author: hackermailman
story_title: Why are Soviet math textbooks so hardcore in comparison to US textbooks? (2017)
why: CMU discrete math lecture solving problems collaboratively with the class.
quote: CMU Discrete Math course has kind of the same techniques where he solves problems with the whole class [VIDEO]
text:
Bulgarian/USSR Math Circles [LINK] and problems they work on are in this book [LINK]

Regular school you would solve problems in combinatorics, algebra and geometry together in class by offering small ideas or strategies then trying each one to point out what works and doesn't work. You do enough of these everyday in class then reasoning about abstract sets in analysis isn't a huge leap. Same reason we used to read Euclid in class and make students demonstrate countless proofs.

CMU Discrete Math course has kind of the same techniques where he solves problems with the whole class [VIDEO]

The best students then joined the school math circle with professional mathematicians and became TAs like in university helping their regular class.

They tried and failed the soviet curriculum with New Math [LINK]

Singapore high school students learn the equivalent of AP Calculus in Grade 10 then either spend years 11/12 at a trade school or stay to earn an associates degree to prep for university covering engineering electives like linear algebra and differential equations.

story_title: Pico CSS is no longer maintained
why: Kevin Powell's CSS Grid approach to container and breakout layouts.
quote: The layout approach is based on this Kevin Powell video: [VIDEO]
text:
Sounds like that older Vivaldi version does not support CSS nesting. I looked into it. I'm assuming you are using Vivaldi 5.6 which uses Chromium 108, native CSS nesting became supported in Chromium 112.

The layout approach is based on this Kevin Powell video: [VIDEO]

It uses CSS Grid to create a centered, width-constrained content area while allowing individual elements to break out of it or span the full viewport width. This provides a flexible, consistent layout without the need for additional wrapper elements in the HTML.

CSS nesting has had full browser support for more than 3 years now, I recommend updating. I'll also add fallback for older browsers, but the Grid layout itself isn't the issue.

author: game_the0ry
story_title: Patrick Stewart taught us what good men do with power
why: First Contact scene where Picard explains moneyless future economics.
quote: I love that movie.
text:
There was scene in one of my favorite movies, Star Trek: First Contact.

Not to spoil it too much, but there is a scene where a woman from the past (from the 21st century) gets beamed up to the Starship Enterprise. She asks how much it cost. Full dialog below:

> Lily: "How much did this thing cost?"

> Picard: “The economics of the future are somewhat different. You see, money doesn’t exist in the 24th century.”

> Lily: “No money? You mean you don’t get paid?”

> Picard: “The acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force in our lives. We work to better ourselves and the rest of humanity.”

The 24th century of the Star Trek universe was unburdened by corporate shareholders. Leaders, like Jean-Luc, did not have the carrot of a multi-million dollar bonus, nor the stick of getting fired for missing quarterly expectations. That's why he could lead with total integrity -- the incentives were different, arguably much better.

I love that movie. I named my VPS Hermes agent “borg.”

author: realPtolemy
story_title: Discussion: Will Time-Sharing Return?
why: 1963 view on timesharing solving computer bottlenecks
text:
GPU rental market is definitively a form of time-sharing.
But I expecting larger "compute rental" deals B2B, without middle-men enabling it. For example; Disney renting their compute to American Airlines.

VPS well, yes - but also no, you don't rent your self in on Costcos servers. The "cloud era" arose because the cost of VPS became so much cheaper than having all servers stacked in-house, and the fact that they provide easier maintenance and off-loads various data security risks that a regular company would have difficulties to comply with. I.e. higher up-time, lower latency for customers, less data security risks, less maintenance, lower cost.

But what we see with GPUs and AI driven compute, it can effectively be done locally, at a cheaper cost depending on the quantity of compute, requires little maintenance, the output can be offloaded on a cloud hosted VPS, the customer interface can still be routed through a cloud hosted VPS, but from a data security perspective you may deem it to be less risky to run local models on local compute.

I guess you could see XAI's (XSI's?) deal with Anthropic for compute as a sort of time-sharing, but I expect us to see these kind of deals being brokered between "non-tech" companies - unless token costs fall dramatically and unless it'll be truly ensured that all token processing is conducted in fully encrypted and closed of environments that are not used for training at all.

author: Wowfunhappy
story_title: Anthropic blocks users for anything touching training larger models
why: Claude Opus building a music video via JavaScript animations
quote: see Claude Opus 5.5 creating a music video, via building animations in Javascript
text:
> They have made a pragmatic decision already to cut loose a whole swathe of users so they can pursue areas higher up the value chain. that was essentially the original decision they made when they went after software engineering instead of general users.

...I don't think I agree that this happened. Claude Cowork exists, as does Claude Design.

My read of Anthropic's strategy is to focus on coding as a means of achieving capability in other domains, via writing code. I would say that's paying off: see Claude Opus 5.5 creating a music video, via building animations in Javascript. [VIDEO]

By writing bits of code, Claude can organize your calendar, create vector graphics, organize your tasks, and so on.

If what you mean is that newer Claude models are worse at creative writing—okay, but to what extent were LLMs ever seriously useful for this, beyond generating slop no one actually wants to read? Opus 3 is still available in claude.ai if you want to use it.

---

Now, separately, I do think that Anthropic is internally obsessed with "existential risk", to the point where they will cut off users. I do think this is genuine based on everything we've heard from Anthropic employees.

And of course, this safety culture likely persists in part because it's also useful to the company's overall strategy, in the same way Apple's focus on user privacy, while likely genuine, conveniently lets them maintain control of the App Store.

text:
Well, Greg KH emphatically states that local LLMs are more than good enough for bug finding in the Linux Kernel. [0] Seems strong enough for the task to me. [1]

He goes on to recommend that one uses local LLMs exclusively for bug finding because he and his colleagues have seen multiple occasions where folks who used the LLMs provided by the Major LLM Manufacturers had the stuff they were working on get "mysteriously" leaked.

Even if that sort of thing were not known to happen, it's just smart to not process data you want to keep secret in systems that are known to straight up retain user data and/or "anonymize" user data and send it back to their HQ for use in production of newer versions of their products.

[0] IIRC, it is this video: 

[1] And even if they're six months behind the latest publicly-available tools provided by the Major LLM Manufacturers, six months ago a notable subset of folks were on here screaming that their latest tools enabled fully-automated hands-off coding and had ushered in an era of Software Factories that were rapidly going to make all programmers obsolete. ;)

author: perching_aix
story_title: CVE-2026-98432: Linux TCP Use-After-Free Risk and Patch Validation
why: Kernel maintainer's view on LLMs as bug finders
quote: From the horse's mouth, in case you were suspecting these descriptions to be in bad faith
text:
You severely underestimate humanity's goalpost moving capabilities.

The state of cope:

- models are still not intelligent, they're just like, uhh, really good semantic fuzzers! so you can just put them in the loop, they'll fuzz your code, and all is good :)

- the number of bugs is "finite", so - esp with agentic help - we'll just catch up and all will be good :)

Annoyingly, the cope frontier is kinda right about both of these, so the joke shall go on. The only real counter to it would be to bring up that this finiteness claim only really applies to a frozen set of security boundaries and attack surfaces, but they'll probably just raise this being "an academic tier concern" and just tell you to ""fuzz"" more.

So ironically, it looks like these practices are rescued once again, and the bare minimum stays winning. It also starts being moved to the territory of the magic box, but I guess nobody cares about that anymore. Local AI will just get really good too, fully competitive and self hostable even. Any day now.

From the horse's mouth, in case you were suspecting these descriptions to be in bad faith: [VIDEO]

"secure implementation" is vague, for example, here is an OpenCode issue (links to related PRs/follow ups) that I worked with their team through to improve security.

Our hunch is that the Ai told them this was ok to do, but it broke invariants users relied on. Perhaps it was not "hackable" in the sense I think you are getting at, but it did open a very big security hole through choices and design. The critical thinking was lacking (imo).

[LINK]

The bots make mistakes all the time, even through multiple rounds of reviews. Thus I have zero faith that they will produce secure code reliably 100% of the time. More Ai does not magically fix this, they go down the wrong path and double down, or work around incorrect assumptions.

Also worth noting that OpenCode Console was hacked days after the configuration regression and two PRs to change it back. Notable because it shows a pattern.

story_title: Pointing AI at archives found a forgotten meteorite, lost rhinos, and more
why: Shows AI-found Linux bugs were overstated
quote: This is like the Anthropic people feeling like they found many many "very important" Linux bugs [VIDEO] - hint: no.
text:
This article is NOT like the Dodo or Newton ones. The Dodo author was an expert in Dodos. The Newton one was by a Newton expert. In those cases, it was the relentlessness of the AI that found edge cases that were interesting.

But Here, the start is "What field should I approach and what questions should I ask?"

But this is NOT the same!

When I watch my non-tech friends vibe-coding, I'm struck by how they are so ignorant of basic tech stuff, but little tiny bubbles of "experience" start to percolate in them after a while. Things like "wait, I think this project has weird dependencies that are going to cause trouble when I move it to my office machine" or "hold on, the mobile version doesn't share the same text with the desktop version?"

It is much less interesting to have an attitude of "I don't know or care, just give me a 'result'" vs "Aha! I see where we could apply this in a productive way!"

This is like the Anthropic people feeling like they found many many "very important" Linux bugs [VIDEO] - hint: no.

When it's something you know about, the overstating is obvious! It's only when you don't know about things that shallow work (or slop) feels significant.

author: Kotlopou
story_title: Jules Verne's Lost Novel
why: Diner scene from Scorsese's After Hours that hooked the commenter.
quote: One of the best film-watching experiences I've had recently was After Hours
text:
I don't understand the supposed value of AI-made art tailored to the viewer's wishes. One of the best film-watching experiences I've had recently was After Hours, which I got sent to by some random online article linking to a scene [1]. I would never have asked for this film or been able to describe it without having seen it. My favorite book of all time is One Hundred Years of Solitude, which I was forced to read in high school (balancing out all of the other nonsense they made us read) -- it's set in a small Colombian town and has about as little to do with my life (in a capital city in Central Europe) as imaginable. I love the webcomic 1/0 [2], whose author was a creationist when writing it (I found it as an insufferable atheist kid).

We find art that is fun and interesting and unexpected and it expands what we are. That's one of the purposes of art. Watching something predictable eventually gets your survival boredom instinct to kick in. Is this not a common experience?

story_title: Brief History of PDP Computers
why: Video about Doug Humphrey (DIGEX), early ISP founder.
quote: The Digex Video! - Part 1:
text:
That's what I think too. The VAX is a lot more like the PDP-11 than the PDP-10. Hard core 36-bit PDP-10 programmers (like DIGEX, who I quoted in response to Walter's comment) were dismissive of and looked down on the 32 bit VAX.

Doug Humphrey's nickname was DIGEX, and he had a PDP-10 in his living room in Westchester Tower Apartments that he acquired from a loading dock at the University of Maryland. author: DonHopkins
story_title: Brief History of PDP Computers
why: Music video of 1969 PIXIE CAD films with first radial menus.
quote: Here's a music video I cut from the 1969 films of that system running on the PDP-7 and Titan at Cambridge.
text:
I just made a PDP-7 and Type 340 vector graphics display emulator that runs in the web browser, based on SIMH, in order to reincarnate and run 128 pages of PDP-7 assembly language source code listings of a CAD system called PIXIE written at Cambridge by Heinz Lemke.

It also boots PDP-7 UNIX, the one this article is about. Log in as ken, password ken:

[LINK]

Same cabinet runs DECUS DUEL (the spacewar), DEC's light pen test, a lunar lander, and guess-the-number, besides PIXIE and the Forth below.

Here's a music video I cut from the 1969 films of that system running on the PDP-7 and Titan at Cambridge. PIXIE has the first known radial menus:

[VIDEO]

Cambridge librarian David Chapman digitized the uncut films from the Cambridge University Library:

[LINK]

[LINK]

The listing the emulator runs was assembled 12 February 1972. I wanted to look and feel first hand how the radial menus work, so here's that code running in the browser:

[LINK]

Here's the PDP-7 assembly source code I recovered. The page runs the image it assembles to:

[LINK]

I asked Mitch Bradley, who is the Forth guru who wrote OpenFirmware, if there was a Forth system for the PDP-7, so in one day he and Claude created one, including a Turtle Graphics library for the Type 340 vector graphics display! It turns out that the PDP-7 instruction set is perfect for Forth, and its inner interpreter loop is only three instructions.

Mitch Bradley's PDP-7 Forth:

author: verdverm
story_title: The federated code forge
why: ATProto private data working group discussion of authorization designs
quote: I shared my vision for what it could have been in the first ATProto Private Data WG
text:
Spaces left a number of core authorization building blocks out of the protocol. Those will need to be implemented in "user space" and I expect a number of different approaches will be attempted. I also expect this to become fragmented.

I shared my vision for what it could have been in the first ATProto Private Data WG: [VIDEO] (basically Zanzibar, UCANN is also interesting) I have ideas for a new protocol that would be permissioned, more federated, but still draw on the good parts of atproto. It's geared towards small social (think discord server / facebook groups) than big social (most common apps we think of - with reposts, quotes, blocks - features I have sworn off).

The Bluesky team didn't join the conversation until pretty late and then picked their own proposal (blog post series, was not formal at that point).

author: rvanderlinden
story_title: Show HN: Overtone – Transcribe, correct and cut captions for any screen shape
why: Example of Netflix visual localization across languages
quote: Netflix does this as well, they did it for a Mexican show called Ctrl-Z
text:
Netflix does this as well, they did it for a Mexican show called Ctrl-Z: [VIDEO]

And here's an example of the Warner Bros. movie Demolition Man, where they localized Pizza Hut product placement outside of the US:
[LINK]
(even the logos on the door were paintbrushed away, there's more clips to be found on YouTube btw)

Both Netflix and Disney push development of the Interoperable Master Format (IMF). I haven't seen visual localization happen outside of those two.

The John Wick movies have "expressive" closed captions, which as far as I know they've done in both English and Spanish. Other languages get forced narrative subtitles, sometimes with and sometimes without the English burnt-in captions.

And about the future: GenAI could definitely help localize parts of the video. Wouldn't surprise me if it's been used for this already. Combine that with IMF and you've got a solution that can instantly be adopted in the high-end production world.

author: llm_nerd
story_title: Product Managers aren't safe either
quote: What would you say you do here? - [VIDEO]
text:
What would you say you do here? - [VIDEO]

Gen AI has changed every single part of classic software development, and the impact hasn't even remotely been felt. And zero jobs are "safe" in that traditional way that we saw them.

It's actually staggering to think of how the teams I've led developed software five years ago, ten years ago, fifteen years ago and twenty years ago. Easily 95% of that effort has been obliterated (I'm estimating on the low side, more like 99.5%). Classic wisdom like "the specification needs to be 100% up front because once we implement it stratifies" are relics of the past.

Everything has changed. I can't fully express how software development will work, but it certainly won't involve someone whose job is "human interaction".

author: jauntywundrkind
story_title: The federated code forge
why: How small, cheap relays can aggregate an entire open social network.
quote: Paul has a talk on designing for scalability
text:
You already could host either the web app, the knot (the repo), or the spindle (the runner) yourself, they were just harder to run yourself. I think it says a lot of good things that you can one by one pick which pieces of the system you want to host where!

It is a social network so I'm not sure what the issue about yes needing to read the network is. There are really good relays designed to help aggregate and filter the network. They can run on $5 VPS, processing the entire network, which is awesomely cheap, not just Tangled, which is awesome, what I would call a huge win. Paul has a talk on designing for scalability, about how it's possible to have such small boxes doing the network aggregation with so little resources, that appviews can then consume their interests from. solving for scale in open social networks, [VIDEO]

The servers are definitely not keeping the whole network. The post talks to this some, but the new Knot2 retains a local copy of repo-relevant material (comments prs etc) in its own git tree, that collects what the network has done together, and makes it easy to ship/replicate, while also using that as a sync source to replicate back into atproto too, to make network visible.

Agreed that I really wish ForgeFed were showing much more clear progress. It seems like such a good idea, but it's been a number of years now and it's super murky what the progress is and where we are. Having >1 viable player in the decentralization of forges would be great. I have

So many thoughts and memories...here are some:

First time watching Star Trek in Tunisia in the early 1990s. It was a very hot summer, and the air-conditioned basement of my friend’s folks contained every episode of The Original Series and The Next Generation, and a computer with games like Rogue, as well as American junk food like sour cream and onion chips and cherry-vanilla ice cream, so we spent quite a bit of time there :D

Star Trek TNG’s optimistic view of humanity overcoming its primitive base instincts.

Videogames and VR as nascent versions of the holodeck.

Facepalm, [PicardTips]([LINK]), etc.

Quotes, conversations, monologues, including [Data’s about death]([VIDEO]), with the butterfly.

Background [hum]([LINK]) of the Enterprise, Ressikan Flute in [The Inner Light]([LINK]).

“[More familiarity with our own mythology may help us relate to theirs]([LINK]).”

Jokingly speaking in stentorian English, like a captain, while riding on a boat. A young person asks me where I learned to speak like that. Answer: Watching Jean-Luc Picard in TNG, and reading some VVilliam The Spear Shaker!

[LINK]

> “There is a tide in the affairs of men, which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune; omitted, all the voyage of their life is bound in shallows and in miseries. On such a full sea are we now afloat, and we must take the current when it serves, or lose our ventures.”

> “Seize the time... Live now! Make now always the most precious time. Now will never come again.”

Goodby

author: GlobalChubby
story_title: AI isn't replacing SREs, it's deskilling them
why: Aviation lecture on automation dependency and losing manual skills.
quote: I think [VIDEO] might be a good watch
text:
This was just the default where I worked. We called the exercise Wheel of Misfortune: facilitator sets up an outage / bug in a non-prod environment (inspired by real events or not), spins a wheel, picks a victim, and the problem is solved collectively, manually. That's the standard format, but it could be much more freeform than that: the point is to educate each other regarding "incident management."

I will say, I'd always been skeptical that AI could be better at incident management than an experienced engineer with deep domain / institutional knowledge, but I was recently proven wrong: Claude root-caused and helped resolve a Postgres lock queue pileup that I believe would have taken me much longer to fix.

Re: aviation being a perfect industry to learn from, I think [VIDEO] might be a good watch. I was introduced to this at a Wheel of Misfortune around 5 years ago, so it's interesting watching it today when AI is encroaching upon everything.

text:
Children of the Magenta Line seems very topical, especially wrt AI

>In 1997, American Airlines captain Warren VanderBurgh gave a lecture warning about the dangers of autopilot. He titled it "children of the magenta line," after the magenta coloured course line the flight computer draws across a cockpit display. He noticed that pilots were so used to following that line, to managing the automation rather than actually flying the plane, that they lost their own skills to manually fly the plane. This wasn’t a problem until it was a problem.

>VanderBurgh’s concern was not about autopilot itself but rather the complete dependency on autopilot at the expense of the internal knowledge of how it works and the loss of the judgment to know when to use it. In 2009, his warning came true in the very worst way possible over the Atlantic. When Air France 447’s sensors iced over, the autopilot handed a perfectly good airliner back to its crew, the pilots, confused and out of practice, stalled it into the sea.

The ideology is amazing.

The terminology is terrible.

But yes. When they say land they actually mean "natural resource".

The idea is that human-made resources should have their profits go to humans, but natural resources (most notably location value) do not belong to humans because humans did not make them, and also, the economic incentives normally associated with markets such as supply/demand management and price discovery don't apply because supply can't change.

Its extremely economically efficient and is endorsed by many economic thinkers on both the right and the left, as well as many social justice activists.

text:
I host a podcast for senior engineers and leaders, and recently interviewed Mark Allen (Head of Engineering at Junction).

I really liked his take on underperformers:

- He thinks the "spend 10% of your time on underperformers" rule doesn't survive reality. Every case is different.

- If you're having the same one-to-one 3 or 4 weeks in a row with no change, then its time to escalate it.

- Be explicit about whether their role is at risk, based on how your company actually works.

- Give it about two cycles of work (two projects, however long that is where you work) before considering an exit.

Full episode: [VIDEO]

story_title: Herdr has released native app
why: The original 1980 Calvin Klein 'nothing between' commercial
quote: They're unironically echoing the infamously iconic 1980 Calvin Klein jeans commercial
text:
> A new kind of agent workspace. Native and terminal first, with nothing between you and your agents. Every part of it is a plain folder your agent can rewrite, and every agent keeps running when the window is gone.

They're unironically echoing the infamously iconic 1980 Calvin Klein jeans commercial starring a perversely sexualized underaged 15-year-old girl:

"You want to know what comes between me and my Calvins? Nothing." -Brooke Shields

[VIDEO]

Except in this case, the romanticized "nothing" between you and your autonomous agents is a massive, multi-layered stack of legacy Unix abstractions, sockets, remote procedure calls, historic terminal emulators, escape codes, pseudo-tty device drivers, and modern infrastructure slop.

The reality of what is actually sitting between you and your agents:

- A herdr-core background daemon handling JSON-RPC IPC messages.

- A crates/ghostty-sys Rust FFI layer binding against libghostty-vt.

- A hardware-accelerated GPU rendering pipeline drawing terminal cell glyphs.

- A legacy Unix PTY subsystem providing master/slave pairs and terminal line discipline.

- An ancient mountain of VT100/ANSI escape codes and termios settings, with resize requests traveling through IPC and SIGWINCH signals notifying Unix terminal applications.

- A structured agent-status protocol carried by yet another terminal escape sequence, OSC 7501, then exposed through JSON-RPC.

author: rhdunn
story_title: We're releasing the weights of Mistral Large 4
why: Explains residual connections in deep networks
quote: [2] [VIDEO] "The most cited paper of the century is a brilliant hack"
text:
AFAICT there are several things that affect the size of the model:

1. the number of transformer layers -- e.g. each layer adds the ability to provide more information to the residual stream [1], [2]; each layer is `tokens * features * active context`

2. the number of tokens -- the more tokens there are the more word fragments and Unicode characters you can represent

3. the number of features assigned for a token -- these are used to associate trained semantic information for the token; with the active context this can encode contextual information for that token (the idea being that the model can differentiate senses of a word like "bank" depending on its context, so "bank (river)" will have different weights than "bank (building for money)")

4. the active context -- this is the number of `token * features` to include when predicting the next token

One of the key features of LLMs and transformer architectures is that training across different languages helps the model learn the underlying concepts and associations, so training on English only would lose that.

A better approach may be something like a byte architecture or a model where the tokenization is trained with the model (similar to vision and audio) instead of as a separate step. Or maybe training smaller models longer to take advantage of double descent [3], [4].

[1] [LINK] "Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition"

author: tarpitt
story_title: We won't "just hang out"
why: Wonkavator 'up and out' scene illustrating escape metaphor.
quote: I'm attached to the idea that only the way out of this is up and out.
text:
Technology is this one-way ratcheting mechanism which will crush everything dignified within its trajectory. I'm attached to the idea that only the way out of this is up and out. That the solution is to escape into something(?) hyperreal that confounds the assumptions of our unescapable problem.

Not cyberspace or VR as we know it, but maybe something more real than that. Something that is limited in the way reality is limited.

>People used to settle towns in the dirt when they scarcely had anything to eat and what, we now can't open a community center, or a maker space?

text:
Misheard words is something that Overtone fixes. But it can't fix all, in some cases audio mix and pronunciation are so bad that it's genuinely hard even for a human in their native language to understand. Music also messes up speech-to-text models.

Unfortunately translation of (on-screen) text wasn't built into Overtone. This is something both Netflix and Disney are very aware of, and they already create multiple visual versions of content. On both platforms you can trigger a different visual language version by changing your UI language. Disney movies are most known for this: [VIDEO]

They use the IMF format to transport content with "overlays" for different languages. In those languages certain frames are swapped out for a translated version. So that an EXIT sign is seamlessly translated to a SALIDA sign in Spanish for example.

Simpler way to do this is forced narrative captions. They are basically a separate captions track to only translate stuff like the on-screen sign you mention. This is combined with regular captions. Netflix turns them on by default I believe, and on Apple TV+ it's called "auto" captions.

The core problem is that AI isn't yet able to do everything. There's a race to the bottom going on for translation companies and things won't get better until AI gets better probably. why: IPv6 address planning talk illustrating address space scale

text:
Ran across a comment a while ago on some fun "IPv6 math":

 On the surface of the Earth [land+water], there are 8.4 IPv4 addresses per km². Not counting the oceans, that would be 28 IPv4 addresses per km² land.

 IPv6 gives 10¹⁷ addresses per mm² (yes, square millimetre).

 In terms of volume, 10⁸ IPv6 addresses per mm³ throughout the Earth.

* Via: [LINK]

A second way of thinking about it:

* Stars in the Milky Way: 400 Billion

* Galaxies in the universe: 2 Trillion

* So (4x10¹¹)x(2x10¹²) = 8x10²³ stars in the universe.

* Size of IPv6 address space: 3.4x10³⁸

* Find the ratio between addresses and stars: 3.4x10³⁸ / 8x10²³

IPv6 offers about 430 trillion times more addresses than estimated stars in the universe. From Tom Coffee's presentation "An Enterprise IPv6 Address Planning Case-Study":

Windows didn't ship with a competent PDF reader for over a decade and some because of the DOJ: Any attempt by Microsoft to enter a market that already had a competition was seen as anticompetitive.

It's pretty trivial to get ValidationOS running, even down to RL1 where the kernel and NT execution environment are the only things you have: [VIDEO]

author: npunt
story_title: MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display and Touch
why: Jobs' trucks vs cars analogy for Mac vs iOS
quote: it's the truck that does the heavy work so the other platforms like iOS are light [1]
text:
That's never been Apple's market, B2B is not in their DNA, nor is winning absolute market share. You're asking them to go from being a company that is about something (great consumer experience) to a company that chases profit wherever it can find it.

Once they go down that path, they open themselves up to whatever technology changes and drifts happen in an entirely different market, which right now is going through a tectonic shift with AI. We don't even know what happens in that market in 1-2 years let alone 5 or 10 or more. The business cycles are different, the customers are different, the demands are different. How do you even begin to plan for that?

You're zeroing in on a technical advantage Apple currently has with silicon while ignoring the lack of advantage they have everywhere else in their operation. That'll never happen and it's the antithesis of a half century of company history.

As far as the Mac, it's the truck that does the heavy work so the other platforms like iOS are light [1]. That's been the guiding philosophy, the sandbox it plays within.

[1]: [VIDEO]

author: nrposner
story_title: Software is slow because of bad design, not slow languages
why: Evidence that low latency increases user retention and spending.
quote: fast, smooth interaction measurably increases user retention and spending
text:
More often than you might think: low latency on interactions, loads, responses, etc is a high priority for e.g. social media sites and online marketplaces, where fast, smooth interaction measurably increases user retention and spending ([link]([VIDEO])).

Also the case for desktop applications: lower latency on input directly improves user experience and satisfaction. Some applications directly market based on this: half of the Zed editor's marketing is 'coding at 4k 144FPS'.

Though you might not immediately think of it as 'software' gamedev is one of the most performance-focused regions of the industry, especially in graphics, especially especially for studios building or customizing their engines. Reducing memory consumption lets you comfortably increase scope, making the engine more efficient increases your frame count. A bad framerate on console/mid-range PCs alone can be the touch of death for a project.

In cases where the software isn't end-user facing, performance is still often a concern even when there isn't a strong real-time constraint, not just because of temporal latency, but because slow software means more time spent running the software, which means paying for more servers or a higher cloud bill. A badly optimized core cloud pipeline can devour an org's budget, where a well-optimized one can run for peanuts.

story_title: Creating interactive data visualization with Flint-interactive
why: Demo of Flint-interactive charts for AI agents
text:
Since we last built Flint earlier this year ([LINK]), we have been wondering if interactive charts can also find they home in terms of simple high-level specifications to allow AI agents to produce them easily, reliably and with high-quality. I have always been amazed by NYT interactive stories back in school, as they can always tell a fun story without super long verbose text write-ups; thus I have been wondering what if they can just be as easily created as any basic charts to make them easier to create everywhere.
Despite the AI models now are more capable of creating interactive artifacts, we find creating interactive charts still kinda annoying (esp. if you are building them to serve users directly in their chat, in your data apps). Agents (especially with smaller models) quite often generate interactions with undesired effects, they are often quite slow, costly, and extremely annoying if to want to steer it to change something. Most times, I find that if I ask the agent to change interaction, it can randomly change style, layout, even the data.

We find the issue is that the language agents use to create interactive visualization is kinda low-level. The logic for specifying data encoding, style and interactions are all entangled (if you swap x,y axis, you are likely going to redo your interaction and layout again). quote: (that was presented at Devoxx
text:
A sad day for CPython but it doesn't have to be a sad day for Python. There is a fully maintained implementation of Python 3.13 that has an advanced JIT compiler. Once your Python warms up it can be 4x faster or higher (depending on what your program is doing). That implementation is called GraalPy and it builds on the JVM:

[LINK]

A bit like Chrome there's a fully open source version and a proprietary version with a few extra bells and whistles, but the latter is entirely free for both open and commercial usage (you can't redistribute it for a fee). So you may as well use it.

It has other interesting features

• Scalable pauseless GC

• Single binary distribution of Python programs (like Go)

• Fancy and optimized interop with other languages including Java, JavaScript, Kotlin, Ruby and any other Truffle language.

• Supports native extensions. Tested and works with common libs like SciPy, NumPy, PyTorch, Pandas etc: [LINK]

• They're working on a GIL-free mode

In recent weeks there has been a release of a new web framework for Python that only runs on GraalPy, called Pyronaut ([LINK]). It takes advantage of JVM interop to expose the Micronaut framework, which is similar to Spring for those who know it. Thanks to the JIT and well optimized base libraries it runs extremely fast, being about 3x faster than FastAPI+Granian, or 7x faster than Flask+Gunicorn and having many more features.

[VIDEO]

story_title: Show HN: Pinscope – remote access, logs and OTA for ESP32 in 9.4KB of RAM
why: Demo of Pinscope ESP32 remote access, logs and OTA
quote: Video: [VIDEO]
text:
Hi HN!

I’m the developer behind Pinscope. I have always found TLS’s memory footprint to be a challenge when working with the ESP32, making it nearly impossible to integrate TLS-based remote control in some memory-constrained projects.

Demo: [LINK]

Video: [VIDEO]

Source: [LINK]

That is one of the reasons I built Pinscope. It enables remote access, OTA, crash reports, and debug logs to ESP32 devices behind NAT, using Noise protocol for secure connection with minimal memory footprint. It requires only 9.4KB of RAM and can be integrated in any ESP32 project in just a single line of code.

The client code is public, but it is not open source and the free plan supports up to three devices.

I’d love to hear your feedback!

story_title: Three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics
why: Chomsky and Foucault debate on human nature
text:
Ok my original comment was snarky (apologies to all three mods), but you've raised one of my favorite topics so I can't resist engaging a bit more seriously! In the second clause, that is -- the first is trivially true in some senses and trivially false in others, so it doesn't seem very productive to nail down.

So Chomsky thought of himself as a philosopher of science more than anything, and his life mission is/was to answer a fascinating question: what kind of creatures are we? There's been a growing consensus going back to at least Darwin that we're separated from the rest of Animalia by our "reason" (!= intuition != understanding != judgement != volition), but he helped popularize an old theory[1] that puts it kind of beautifully: human language is only possible in beings capable of producing an infinite set of meaningful outputs in response to a finite input.[2] And so far, that list includes only two definite members: Homo sapiens sapiens, and computer programs built upon large language models.[3]

So all that to say: yes, I think you're wrong; the programmatic ensembles that brought us today's breakthroughs are an "infinitely deep well". As long as we have questions to ask, they are not theoretically constrained from answering them.

author: boumedinebillal
story_title: Show HN: Live speech-to-text on an ESP32-P4 microcontroller, no cloud
why: Demo of live offline speech-to-text on an ESP32-P4
quote: Hi HN, I'm the author.
text:
Hi HN, I'm the author. This runs an open-vocabulary English speech recognizer live on an ESP32-P4: you speak into the board's mic and the words appear on its screen as you talk. No network, no NPU: just the chip's two RISC-V cores and their SIMD extension (PIE).

The model is Kroko (by Banafo), a 65.7M-parameter streaming Zipformer2 transducer. As released it is 71 MB in int8, which does not fit the board's 32 MB of PSRAM, so I quantized the weights to 2 and 4 bits (26.65 MB, groups of 128 with a Hadamard rotation, the bit width chosen per matrix) and wrote my own engine: integer arithmetic throughout, with the hot loops hand-written in PIE assembly.

Numbers, measured on all of LibriSpeech:

test-clean 4.34% WER, test-other 10.26% (the original int8 model on a PC: 3.94% and 9.17%).

1.28 s of audio processed in 0.90 s (0.70x real time), both cores at 400 MHz.

A word is final about 2 s after it is spoken.

One thing I care about: the chip computes exactly the same bits as the engine's PC build, so every accuracy number above is the chip's, not a simulation. Getting there meant replacing libm (newlib and glibc disagree in the last bit of log/exp/cos) with deterministic math on both sides.

There are also hotwords (phrases to listen for, from a text file on the SD card) and six voice-control demos driven by simple word rules, no LLM.

Limits: English only; it needs the chip revision v3 (P4X) with 32 MB PSRAM; accuracy is measured on clean read speech, noisy rooms not yet. You

I ended up selling a lot of my L mount gear and consolidating on Nikon for professional work.

story_title: US designates helium as a critical material
why: Interview on helium shortage, uses, and production challenges
quote: Good interview on the subject on Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast
text:
Good interview on the subject on Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast a few months back, "Now There's a Helium Shortage and It Affects More Than Balloons":

> Ripple effects from the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz continue to widen. There's yet another brewing shortage, this time in helium. While most people associate helium with balloons and funny voices, the element is used in a surprisingly wide variety of industrial settings, including semiconductor production, where its role in advanced lithography has been growing rapidly. But helium mining and exploration in North America has been practically non-existent for a variety of reasons. And while the US used to have a strategic helium reserve, the government started selling that down in the late 1990s. On this episode, we speak with Nicholas Snyder, the founder and CEO of North American Helium, which does helium mining in Canada. Yeah, you're referring to Scott Meyers and he gave a really insightful talk about how complex and inconsistent C++ has become here titled "The Last Thing D Needs":

[VIDEO]

Slides are here:

[LINK]

The conclusion is "The last thing D needs is someone like me." meaning D should avoid designing a language where you basically need a niche of lawyers crawling through the language standard to decipher the meaning of various features and then write about how to safely use those features. It's not that languages shouldn't have experts who give good advice, but that the nature of advice in C++ has come down to explaining arbitrary rules, inconsistencies, and obscure corner cases rather than how to use the language effectively to solve actual problems.

He says at some points (taken from the transcript):

"There are some arbitrary, wacky decisions, in my opinion ... There's a lot of, in my opinion, simple arbitrary choices that did not have to be made that make explaining things more complicated and also make working with the tool more complicated."

"Much too much of what I've written about has been tool use, talking about language idiosyncrasies, arbitrary decisions, things you need to be able to remember."

"There is epicycle on epicycle on epicycle inside this language."

And then he followed it up a few years later with a blog post explaining that he won't be updating his book with language related fixes because he no longer trusts himself to know what's right from what's wrong

author: andrecasal
story_title: I don't know if this page explains why the product exists
why: Demo of Durabl, an AI-ready boilerplate codebase with rules to prevent drift
quote: I've built this product and page and I don't know if it explains why it exists clearly.
text:
Right so... I've built this product and page and I don't know if it explains why it exists clearly.

I've been developing with AI pretty much since it came out. The problem with coding with AI is that you inevitably get to a point where you just feel like throwing your codebase in the trash and starting over.

The AI stays stuck spending tokens on a bug it created itself. I know mine has.

So I came up with this idea: build a codebase that already has everything I need built in (so essentially a good boilerplate or starting position with auth, payments, a complete ui library, the works) but also built-in rules for the AI so it doesn't drift. This is the really important thing: rules like "There's only one way of doing something in this codebase" and "Rely on TypeScript type inference whenever possible, but fully type objects across boundaries (network, localStorage, user input, etc); never use `:any`". So, good practices for coding so I'm proud of the code it actually outputs, but also guidance on the architecture and on how to manage its own internal AI memory system. That memory tells it what to read before it plans, what architecture not to change later, and how to manage the memory itself. Plus tools (control Chrome, connect to Higgsfield, etc), skills (SEO, AEO, UI, design, marketing, writing, etc), guides (one-off guides for your AI to set things up when you need to — Resend, Sentry, Google Analytics, etc), the works.

What is more macho, changing your baby's diaper, or expecting your wife to do it? Changing a diaper is a woman's job.

Over on the entertainment side, video is getting really good. Yes, there's a huge amount of AI slop, but the good stuff is quite good.

- Kono Express. [1] Disney laid off an character animator from the Star Wars factory. The animator decided to see what was possible with the best modern tools. He's using both AI tools and Unreal Engine. There are six episodes now, and each one is a bit better than the last, as he gets a handle on the technology. The first episode looks like generic sci-fi stuff, at good quality but not yet perfect. By episode three, he has this nailed. It keeps getting better. Episode six [2] is a delight. He's now almost up to current Hollywood quality. One person, turning out half an hour of content every few weeks. Who needs Disney any more?

- Asian vertical dramas. 17,000 episodes per day. Apparently 55% of China's AI capacity is cranking these out. Search for "asian drama creation tools". Amusingly, Google and Bing have completely different tool lists. These are all software as a service products, with accounts and token charges. Currently, visuals are quite good, with some notable errors. Complex patterns on clothing don't stay consistent, for example. Continuity errors remain common.

After a few days of processing the initial shock, I was able to get to work and rage-code MoaV -- still ongoing at the time of writing -- which is a modular anti–internet censorship stack, able to run 10+ internet censorship circumvention tools on a small VPS or Raspberry Pi, with the goal of democratizing VPN provisioning. author: noufalibrahim
story_title: fheroes2: A recreation of Heroes of Might and Magic II game engine
why: LLM fumbling through Police Quest 1 via custom harness
quote: It's silly how much it fumbles whereas 15 year old me could beat the game fairly quickly.
text:
Interesting. I did the same but with Police Quest 1 (the AGI version). I vibe-coded an AGI interpreter which my harness could drive an had it run the game. I gave it a scan of the manual for initial information. It's silly how much it fumbles whereas 15 year old me could beat the game fairly quickly. [VIDEO]

I did manage to give it information via. screenshots, planning and several other things. Harness engineering is fun to do and a worthwhile exercise. It finally managed to score 93 of 245 points and then just choke out. I figured that a large language model would be able to burn through a 1987 primarily text based game with a primitive parser but it's not as easy as it sounds. My takeaway was that the LLM is definitely intelligent but not "generally" so.

One, it was pre-phone saturation, so the crowd was engaged and the experience was novel. Two, it was astoundingly unique at the time; the production values and concept were just so far forward. For those of you who are younger, it's a little hard to explain, but for me there is "before Alive" and "after Alive" in terms of larger scale electronic music performances. Then of course it becomes really interesting that Random Access Memories really was a fundamental rejection of the beast they'd helped generate. author: Animats
story_title: America has lost 200k of jobs in media, film and the arts. How much is AI?
why: Solo animator's AI/Unreal series nearing Hollywood quality
quote: Episode six [2] is a delight. He's now almost up to current Hollywood quality.
text:
Over on the entertainment side, video is getting really good. Yes, there's a huge amount of AI slop, but the good stuff is quite good.

- Kono Express. [1] Disney laid off an character animator from the Star Wars factory. The animator decided to see what was possible with the best modern tools. He's using both AI tools and Unreal Engine. There are six episodes now, and each one is a bit better than the last, as he gets a handle on the technology. The first episode looks like generic sci-fi stuff, at good quality but not yet perfect. By episode three, he has this nailed. It keeps getting better. Episode six [2] is a delight. He's now almost up to current Hollywood quality. One person, turning out half an hour of content every few weeks. Who needs Disney any more?

- Asian vertical dramas. 17,000 episodes per day. Apparently 55% of China's AI capacity is cranking these out. Search for "asian drama creation tools". Amusingly, Google and Bing have completely different tool lists. These are all software as a service products, with accounts and token charges. Currently, visuals are quite good, with some notable errors. Complex patterns on clothing don't stay consistent, for example. Continuity errors remain common.
Automatically generated audio is currently terrible, at least in the English translations.
Plots are so cliche that it's clear people are re-using the same prompts. "Heiress girl returns from countryside" is very popular. Here's a recent drama, about startup working hour

author: Lammy
story_title: A practical guide to AI image generation, from diffusion to agents
why: Yellow Devil fight shows NES sprite/background tile limits
quote: the famous “Yellow Devil” boss fight plays the way it does because only the moving chunks of the Devil's body are composed of Sprite tiles
text:
> Pixel art is a style, not a format

― person who has never attempted to program for a specific retro system.

Peep the graphics hardware limitations of the Nintendo Famicom/NES, for example: [LINK]

You can see these limitations guiding the designs of actual retro games if you know what to look for.

Example: In CAPCOM's Mega Man (1987), the famous “Yellow Devil” boss fight plays the way it does because only the moving chunks of the Devil's body are composed of Sprite tiles. When one of those chunks reaches the opposite side of the screen, that part of the Devil's body becomes drawn with Background tiles instead: [VIDEO]

This is also why the Devil, Dragon, and Wily boss fights (anything larger than a regular Robot Master) take place entirely in a black void — the Background layer is exhausted drawing the bosses and there's nothing left over for actual play-area background.

why: Example of AI trying to run a profitable business
quote: There are/were already some trials done (The famous WSJ/Anthropic one[0])
text:
> What else is left, once all these benchmarks get saturated?

I was thinking this thing quite recently and wish to write a blog post about it but IMO, I believe that the next AI benchmarks would be profitable businessmaking. There are/were already some trials done (The famous WSJ/Anthropic one[0]) and some shop iirc in SF which is doing this and recent example of trying to start a lemonade stand with AI[1]

In my opinion, it can't really get more meta than that plus on the more humour side, it could help these companies make some dollars as they desperately need it.

I always wonder if these AI models can self-autonomously generate profit, why would these AI companies try to let you generate the main profit while you just pay them one time or a very small amount in tokens. Why should these AI giants allow a person to be a middle man in the first place in some sense and instead not just run these agents autonomously.

Maybe it could be because these AI agents might not be the best in such a meta task (money making/business) but as such, it does feel to me that it might be a good benchmark in the first place.

author: wafflemaker
story_title: Mortality Among People with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
why: Ram Dass on accepting dark thoughts and loving yourself
quote: Even your ADHD self without meds, even your depression and dark thoughts.
text:
ADHD meds unlocked a new dimension of -social, normal people- fun previously inaccessible. Hanging out with people without annoying them, not being late to events, remembering to call friends.

But the -crazy- fun is still accessible. I'm more risk aware, but still get the unconventional ideas. And I can always drop meds for a day and have a "high" day with less productivity and more "crazy" ideas. And I don't mean crazy as a negative, more like an adjective that describes it well.

However, it's important to love yourself (and this can be practiced and trained) and all your aspects. Even your ADHD self without meds, even your depression and dark thoughts. [VIDEO]

Also, I went through a lot of meds, and one I ended up with was because the first one made me a little too much "robot" like for my own liking. I'm too used to being "me" and didn't like how much the first one changed me. But I'd rather people try for themselves than have an opinion based on mine.

Edit: moved a coma, added yt link.

Canadians haven't reacted with restraint to Americans in the decades I've been aware of the divide, and this time there has been no restraint at all.

Canadian politicians and media are pursuing a strategy: it's arguable whether it's clever or foolhardy, but what's not arguable is whether it's restrained.

There's a cultural reason why "look how ignorant and stupid Americans are" has been staple Canadian comedy since the latter half of the 20th century. And it has nothing to do with America.

One of the great things about Americans, by the way, is being able to shrug, maybe chuckle along, and let it be for going on decades. That's what comes from being a first-rate global power. Game of Thrones reminded us "the wolf does not concern himself with the opinion of sheep".

And the power dynamic here is such that the analogy is apt.

text:
David Byrne was recently on, of all things, Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast:

> History is littered with ideas that have been tossed aside, only for them to gain relevance at some later date. Think of Moby-Dick: forgotten in Melville's time, but now regarded as the great American novel. Or the work of economist Hyman Minsky, which became influential a decade after his death, when the 2008 financial crisis made “the Minsky Moment” a mainstream term. These are just a couple of the things we talk about with the legendary musician David Byrne on today's podcast. Byrne's new book, Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up, looks to categorize numerous “sleeping beauties” — ideas that were lost but then rediscovered. Besides Melville and Minsky, we also talk about the lost Roman recipe for concrete and we get into Byrne's thoughts on how to write a song and his own experience of having his music rediscovered by a new generation.

STEVE JOBS: Design's a really loaded word. I don't know what it means. And so we don't really talk about design a lot around here. We actually just talk about how things work. Most people think it's how they look, but it's not really how they look. It's how they work.

Everyone says, you know, I want to make a great product, or I want to make a great movie, or whatever they're doing. So there's no difference there, but there's a big difference in the outcomes.

JONY IVE: When we were developing the new iMac, we were at a point when we had a couple of solutions that, I mean, at the time I think we thought they were good, but we had that sinking feeling, you know, when you are aware that you're trying to convince yourself something's actually better than in your heart you really know that it is. Sometimes you just have to look at yourself and go, you know, it's just not really great. It's okay, it's good, but let's not fool ourselves and call it great.

author: stellar678
story_title: AI and the Enclosure of the Scientific Commons
why: Hopeful look at math careers and economics amid AI advances
quote: Overall it was a lot more hopeful
text:
The discussion of open source was pretty anemic. The author seems to think open source is only GPL copyleft. In reality the vast majority of open source is permissively licensed, and the development was funded by for-profit companies. That seems like a crucial thing to consider when discussing how our information commons has come to be.

Near the end they include a paragraph claiming we should interpret this piece as being about more than self-interest and resistance to change, but it doesn't really feel like the piece offered a taste of what that "more" is.

The most thought-provoking part for me was considering that AI companies have used pretty much all available data for training while "they spend more and more money to create proprietary training data". That seems to break a sort of intuitive social contract - like, well you all used everyone's knowledge. Send yours back out too.

Grant from 3brown1blue released a video exploring the economics and mechanics that enable careers in math, in light of the AI company releases over the last couple weeks. Overall it was a lot more hopeful, and it didn't need to strain awkwardly like this piece to apply an ill-fitting historical framework like enclosure. Worth checking out: [VIDEO]

quote: I feel obligated to quote a comment I saw under 3b1b video
text:
I feel obligated to quote a comment I saw under 3b1b video: [VIDEO]:

I feel like the point is still being missed, and it's very similar to the way software engineers are trying to cope. The argument you are making "Well yes now this part of math we will not need to do again, but now we can do this instead" however the issue with most people just don't want to do that....

Like who are we kidding, the type of nerds who were attracted to math and software were into it because we saw it as an art-form, it was a craft, it was being the only one in your city to be able to solve a complicated math problem, it was immortalizing yourself because you discovered a proof and added to the ever expanding human knowledge.

Imagine a leather workman who's life passion is making insanely high quality handbags, who takes joy in knowing everything he touches will last someone a lifetime and give them joy everytime they use it. And then not gradually, but almost overnight someone comes to his door and tells him we can make bags 50 times better than you at 1/tenth the price. But don't you worry, you can make more money overseeing the factory, or selling people on how good this bag is, and explaining that to them.

I mean, ok, that just is not what I wanted to do with my life. I never wanted to be a manager, I never wanted to be a salesman, I never wanted to be a writer. A craft I enjoy doing has been taken away from me, I should be allowed to mourn, I don't care that I can do something else sin

Now, in the UK most people with a life sentence will (after quite some time) be eligible for parole. Historically it was possible for politicians to block this, but of course the consequence is that if a particularly notorious criminal is scheduled to be paroled, politicians are under pressure to prevent that, while a criminal who didn't attract much public interest leaves on schedule - that's manifestly unfair and a European court told the Brits they can't do that, so eventually the UK's Supreme Court decided there needed to a specific rule, identify a category of people who won't be paroled, and the category they decided on was people who have been convicted of at least two separately conceived murders.

Some good modern jazz I'd recommend (I'm into sax and guitar):

- Julian Lage, exists somewhat in an overlap between jazz/classical/blues [LINK]

- Bill Frisell, no one else sounds like him and his deeply romantic sound [LINK]

- Mary Holvorsen, she's much more avant garde and loves using whacky pedals for effects but still has incredible chops [LINK]

author: ghm2180
story_title: What's Getting Pwned
why: Classic film scene illustrating a bank run
text:
_Most_ people park liquid money in mainstream bank's checking accounts. This money is FDIC insured(upto 250K). The job of this bank is to is money is used by banks to make loans (duh!). There are three "modes" (in increasing yield_ order offered by these banks to account holders:

1. [FDIC] Put it in a Chase, BofA account. < 1% typically. Abysmal returns.

2. [FDIC] A higher yield checking/saving account(Ally at ~3.1 is a good example): But more hoops[1] to get more than 3.5%(today). Here [LINK] the list.

3. [Not FDIC but pretty good**] A higher yield Money market mutual fund. You still need to place a buy order[2]. Something you have to do manually can give you around 3.86% today(See SNAXX)

This last case is more _interesting_ because its easy for agents. But consider what happens when a lot of people use muse to enmasse do this. There can be a run on the banks because[3] its not the same "money" in the balance sheet of the bank. Money leaving checking/savings and entering a MMF is not on the balance sheet of the bank(even though it can be coincidentally the same institution e.g. schwab checkig and schwab brokerage). Agents are a BIG threat to regular banks. I don't even see how it can be prevented, local agents are ubiquitous now.

[1] Exceptions are HY checkings but its hard to chase yield logistically: more hoops to jump like minimum balance or max ceiling, minimum transactions etc.

[2] See this from schwab's site:

author: rafabulsing
story_title: What Is Gridifcation
why: Commenter's mashup built around Earth Wind and Fire's Let's Groove
quote: Link if anyone is interested in checking it out
text:
I dabble in creating mashups from time to time [1] and I see that first hand. One of my first was built around Let's Groove by Earth Wind and Fire. As a funk act, they are as tight as a group of musicians can ever hope to get, and still, the tempo would subtly speed up and down from bar to bar.

It makes things much more challenging to sync up! You can't just speed up the slower song (or vice versa), because even if the averages match, it will still be all over the place from bar to bar. I now have much better workflows to deal with this, but for that first one, I spent a looong time manually adjusting things to get them to fit.

Working with tracks that were recorded to a click (or digitally gridified, as per the article), are much easier to work with. Match the tempos and everything automatically works. Definitely helps creating my mashups...

But I do agree with the post, in that it loses some indescribable human aspect. I love the push and pull of musicians trying to follow each other rather than concentrating on the click. Or even just pushing and pulling against oneself with things like rubato in classical music, sometimes accelerating, and sometimes slowing, at times almost to a dead stop, so as to build a sense of antecip.... pation.

[1] Link if anyone is interested in checking it out: [VIDEO]

story_title: The recently proposed o(n log n) integer multiplication algorithm [pdf]
why: Conway on the unexplained existence of the Monster Group
quote: see John Conway on the Monster Group ("there's never been any kind of explanation for why it's there")
text:
I've seen this claim repeated a bunch of times, it spreads as a meme, but the analogy doesn't work that well. This is not a special feature of biology! Chemical engineering involves lots of trial and error, physics is all about neglecting complicated aspects of a situation and hoping the result is still useful, even fundamental physics has a bunch of cancelations that work with no very good justification (see troubles around renormalization) and then fail when you try to do quantum gravity. Even math has things we know are true but have no good conception of why -- see John Conway on the Monster Group ("there's never been any kind of explanation for why it's there"): [VIDEO]

The whole world has always been like this. It's just showing up with force here.

text:
Agreed, I'd love to see that too!

One criticism I have of HyperCard is that it wasn't "HyperCard All The Way Down", in that not all the rest of its dialogs and user interfaces and menus were made out of HyperCard stacks. It wasn't "metacircular", defined in terms of itself.

That's totally forgivable given that HyperCard was the first original iteration, and "merely" getting it finished in time to ship on every Mac desktop was a spectacular achievement. But it doesn't excuse anything that came after it, and it doesn't excuse Apple for dropping it instead of evolving it.

Cyberdog for OpenDoc was another interesting approach to a web browser, built out of components you could embed in documents, but Apple dropped that along with OpenDoc too:

[LINK]

[VIDEO]

Looking back 30 years, that demo is unintentionally hilarious, and it makes me wonder what HyperCard would have been like if Apple had continued to develop it as much as it deserved.

author: skydhash
story_title: Code is clay now
why: Rich Hickey on correctness, internal machinery versus messy external world
quote: I was watching the most recent Rich Hickey talk[0]
text:
I was watching the most recent Rich Hickey talk[0] and at the start, he talks about correctness and the difference between the internal machinery of your software (which can be finely specified) and handling the external world (which will always be messy).

Good Architecture will try to isolate the two. You got the internal logic which is either the business domain abstracted away. And you got the highly volatile part (request from frontend, new integration, new drivers, deps update,....).

If you've done that, migration/refactoring, unless it entails some unlikely core changes, will not take that long. It's just a matter of dropping that part and replacing it (like changing a car's brake pads or steering wheel). But the actual core mechanism will hardly change over the years.

To go with the thread flow: It's a stone core wrapped by clay.

[0]: [VIDEO]

ADDENDUM

In regards to separation, one of the best example in mind is the OpenBSD kernel code. The OS concepts are in /kern, while each architecture lives in /arch. There's an horizontal separation between machine independent code (core idea of Unix) and machine dependent code (The hardware platform). It can also be found in the various subsystem like audio (the concept of a sound card) and implementation like uaudio (usb interface) and azalia (Intel's HD Audio).

text:
This is indeed what is happening behind the scenes. By default Windows Update will automatically download and install support packages for pretty much any device Windows can identify through manufacturer/device IDs, which includes PCIe and USB devices but also monitors. This is most commonly used to deliver drivers but Microsoft allows these packages to silently install any user-facing application as well, presumably due to peripherals such as GPUs or audio chipsets often requiring "control panels" or similar companion apps.

Around a month ago LG took advantage of this feature by publishing a Windows "driver" for all their TVs and monitors that consisted entirely of payola bloatware, resulting in predictable backlash [1] and the obligatory subsequent HN discussion [2]. None of this has anything to do with the TVs themselves being connected to the internet or not.

story_title: In Hilbert space, all things are quantumly possible
why: Nobel laureates discuss practically exploring Hilbert space
quote: Their discussion may be a good complement to the title article of this thread.
text:
"Hilbert space is the space of all possibilities." -- Wolfgang Ketterle

He gave this pithy summary of his answer to a memorable discussion in a Nobel Laureate panel about what it actually means to explore Hilbert space, from a more practical perspective. Their discussion may be a good complement to the title article of this thread.

Others in this thread already correctly noted that just because something --- 'thing' more precisely defined as some action that results in an observable outcome --- exists in Hilbert space doesn't mean it's possible. But what Ketterle and others were getting at is that, as we make new theories and experiments, we can explore more of Nature and what's possible within, guided by the structure that Hilbert space could give to our questions' outcomes.

That being said, Ketterle explains it much better than I do.

story_title: Show HN: SimCity, but with Permits
why: Argument that suburban development is financially unsustainable
quote: see [VIDEO] for the argument why
text:
They're not popping up anywhere. They're only ever installed in a brand-new development. (Okay, I'm sure somewhere at least one, probably very small, neighborhood has voluntarily formed one for some specific reason, but in general.)

They are in all new developments in most states because the suburb model is financially unsustainable (see [VIDEO] for the argument why), so, if you want to build a nice new development, the town/city is going to say "Who's gonna maintain that little park? Who's gonna cut the grass in the green spaces? Who's gonna sweep the streets?" etc. Not to mention, every amenity outside individual homes (clubhouse, pool, playground) etc. needs to be maintained. Cities can't afford to take them on as public parks, and the individual neighborhoods whose home prices paid for their construction don't really want them to be public either.

And the developer needs to have an entity with which all these responsibilities will vest when they're done building, so, HOA needs to exist.

The alternative is either no shared amenities of any kind, or trying to get the whole city to approve paying for the perpetual maintenance of a new public park when building a new housing tract. Good luck getting that passed, since most existing residents (besides the ones in the next tract over) would say "F that, I'd never go there, why should my taxes pay for it?"

* Config rollback in bootloader to undo mistakes without needing to boot from recovery media

* NixOS integration testing framework (extremely powerful), makes package and config stability better under the hood in nixpkgs

author: applecoffeecake
story_title: You could have invented transformers from memory
why: Shows Villani confused by noise whitening remark around 56:00.
quote: at 56:00 in this video ([VIDEO]), Fields Medalist Cedric Villani is confused by a similar remark about noise whitening
text: The answer is that it just takes continuous and serious engagement with both general and specific mathematics typically through graduate-level courses and research degrees. The particular interpretation of least squares as noise whitening plus orthogonal projection is just a trick you would learn in an advanced statistics class. If you are not versed in the subject, you would not immediately understand the particular math here even as a mathematician! To demonstrate this point, at 56:00 in this video ([VIDEO]), Fields Medalist Cedric Villani is confused by a similar remark about noise whitening and asks the speaker to explain what it means. Here, the speaker is applying the trick to the closely related concept of Linear Minimum Mean Squared Error (LMMSE) estimation which is the probability-theoretic counterpart to least squares. Moreover, Cauchy-Schwarz refers to a fundamental inequality that any mathematician would know, and would show the optimality of orthogonal projection. The general (Cauchy-Schwarz) gives you a foundation for understanding the specific (least squares theory).

author: undefbehavior
story_title: America's new era of private science
why: Short primer on a boundary-testing computation experiment
quote: I produced a documentary exploring this tension
text:
Is the cause of our scientific stagnation primarily tied to funding models (public vs. private), or is it an incentive problem where we simply no longer run boundary-testing experiments?

Maybe the current grant system penalizes experiments where the outcome isn't somewhat known in advance. With all the capital flowing into research, what actual boundary-testing experiments are happening right now? Is it possible to a priori systemically differentiate a boundary test worth doing from a crackpot idea?

I produced a documentary exploring this tension in the context of one scientists potentially boundary pushing OR crackpot idea to test the hard limits of computation (the 3-minute video primer here: [VIDEO], and the full doc: [LINK]).

My question is if we are not running these kinds of high-risk, unknown-upside experiments, what happens when a competing state actor (China) decides to run them first and stumbles into a breakthrough?

Is this just silly?

I think you would have to go back to more classic genetic algorithm/pet training methods: Iterate through increasing "distance" to the goal. Initially make the goal simple/immediately available, then slowly "distance" them from the goal, with more obstacles/etc introduced between, as you go.

For a homing pigeon, this would be literal, driving further and further each time you release them.

For an agent that you train to walk, this would be flat surface to past some line, then introduce speed reward, then non-flat surfaces, then obstacles, then curves, etc [1].

story_title: Gdynia and the Dream of a Maritime Poland
why: Timelapse map of 1000 years of shifting European borders
quote: This is one of my favorite videos about Europe
text:
I have two thoughts here. First, I'm surprised that you're calling out Eastern Europe specifically. This is one of my favorite videos about Europe:

[VIDEO]

The entire continent was basically in a constant state of flux (and perpetual wars) through most of its history, ending with WWII in the West, with the fall of the USSR in most of the Central and Eastern Europe, and then continuing with some regional score-settling in the Balkans.

And even this is a bit reductionist: Spain was a dictatorship until about 1975! How crazy is that. This is basically the recent past of the EU.

For the misery of Central and Eastern Europe specifically, "Bloodlands" by Snyder is a good book. And this gets me to my second point: I think you're veering too far into relativism. Yes, every country did some shitty things - that's the history of the world for ya - but the Russian Empire and the German / Austrian / Prussian Empire can be singled out as especially awful when you look at the past 300-500 years. Even just by the simplest metric of the number of people displaced and killed, it's many orders of magnitude worse than what anyone else has done. This distinction is important because the legacy of bloody imperialism continues on the Russian side today - beyond Ukraine - and it's most certainly not excused by the fact that, dunno, Poland occupied Moscow once.

author: ilamont
story_title: I no longer care to work on any Ruby gems so I've archived all my repositories
why: Claude Opus transcribing a 1918 handwritten diary
quote: A few weeks earlier I worked on an old diary transcription ([VIDEO])
text:
I can't speak to Ruby or other programming languages, but as a creator and occasional hacker with a media background, I have found AI to be incredibly liberating.

Now I can build things that would never have been possible without huge investments of time and/or money. The latest project: a hybrid human/AI tech newsroom that leverages LLM-driven advances in translation ([LINK]).

For my personal passions, LLMs have completely opened up areas that were extremely painful to deal with 5 or 10 years ago. Take genealogy: I used to manually transcribe old letters, and documents in foreign languages (often archaic terms) were impossible for me to work with without seeking out experts. The other night I had an AI go through a book of 200-year-old religious records and pick out references to potential ancestors. A few weeks earlier I worked on an old diary transcription ([VIDEO]) which I later shared with relatives to proof and enjoy. Such tasks are no longer a chore. It's fun again.

The closest comparison I can make was stumbling upon an old HTML tutorial on an MIT website 30+ years ago. All of a sudden, as a writer and creator, I was no longer tied to my employer's business model to get my words and images out to the world.

author: numpad0
story_title: How Quickly Can the DoD Rebuild and Recast the Munitions Industrial Base?
why: Hear the iconic Sidewinder growl tone and lock sequence
quote: American Sidewinder systems use an iconic growling dog[1] tone
text:
Many of Sidewinder style systems use a "tone" to indicate their lock-on state. The tone is low when the system is turned on but not "locked on". It quickly rises into a high pitched tone when it's pointed at something hot. The user is expected to first "cage" the missile, straightening out the sensor, then point it at the target, then "uncage" it and swing around to ensure the change in pitch matches your expectation. Then finally it is to be fired.

We in the public don't have a complete list of missiles from various nations and their tones, but it's well known that American Sidewinder systems use an iconic growling dog[1] tone. Stinger is more sine like[2], and many others appear to be sine like too, and newer systems like 9X and later are clearly just digital and software based even by public descriptions of it.

What I'm suspecting is that, the early gen Sidewinder growl might have been just the raw sensor output piped into the headset, because the operating principle of those seeker units somewhat corresponds to the sounds, down to the high boresight angle warning tone which isn't hard to imagine a kid playing with a benchtop example and accidentally implementing it by damaging some cable.

text:
Sebastian Thrun's talk at Google about winning the DARPA Grand Challenge [0] has a great discussion of training "robots".

Summary:

- the LIDAR had error rates that were not published

- hitting potholes could cause the INS in the car to get confused

- they weren't sure how to fix the errors from the combination of the above

- they ended up just driving the car to generate training data

It worked out well because the computer was predicting if there was an obstacle or not and a split second later the driver of the car would either drive around the real obstacle or the computer would realize that there was no obstacle.

If you've never seen the talk, highly recommend as Thrun is very funny and it's also a time capsule back to when self driving was still a brand new concept.
