author: voidUpdate
story_title: Laptop Based on 6502 CPU
why: Explains Atari 2600 racing-the-beam background drawing without framebuffer
quote: tl;dw - The background is defined with 20 bits
text:
[VIDEO]

tl;dw - The background is defined with 20 bits, which are repeated or mirrored to make the background (eg 00000000111111110000 would either make the background 0000000011111111000000000000111111110000 or 0000000011111111000000001111111100000000). If you write to WSYNC ($D40A), the processor pauses until the start of the next scanline. Then you have to count machine cycles to make sure you modify the background at the right time to make the two halves different. Repeat on each scanline to fully define the background. author: Animats
story_title: SIGSALY: Churchill's top secret hotline to the president
why: 1973 speech digitization samples showing vocoder-like technology
quote: As late as 1973, people were still trying vocoder-like technologies
text:
Here's the technical description, from NSA.[1]

It was really an awful kludge. Today, you'd think, digitize audio into a bit stream, encrypt bitstream. That's not how it worked. It was somewhat similar to the older A-3 analog scrambler, which split up audio into a number of bands and rearranged them, changing the rearrangement occasionally. In SIGSALY, incoming audio was filtered out into 10 frequency bands.
There was also a dominant pitch detector and a "hiss" detector for unvoiced content.
That created 12 analog signals to encrypt. Those signals were much lower bandwidth than the original speech. The patent seems to indicate that the frequency band signals were merely encoded as above or below a threshold. Not a full A/D, just a 1-bit threshold. As late as 1973, people were still trying vocoder-like technologies, but it became easier to work on audio in the digital domain and that died out.[2]

The keying system changed the key every 20ms. It's not clear from the description whether the digitization of the 12 signals was also one sample for 20ms, but it probably was. If you used the same key bits for more than one analog sample, that would create a vulnerability. It's a one time key system, and those only work against serious opposition if the key is only used once. See VENONA.

The articles indicate that synchronizing the key stream, which was on phonograph records, was a huge synchronization headache. Keeping signals in sync was really hard, and was part of the curse of a

story_title: Interactive Linear Programming in the Browser
why: Quick two-minute introduction to linear programming
quote: this two-minute one is pretty good
text:
lpviz visualizes how different linear programming (LP) solver algorithms arrive at their solution, and how they react to adjustments in the problem definition. To start using lpviz you first draw a number of vertices to define the so-called feasible region. Then you point the objective arrow, defining the improvement direction. The answer/optimal point is the point furthest along the improvement direction, while still being inside the feasible region.

LP finds applications in tons of downstream fields, though the typical real-world problem has thousands to millions of variables (whereas lpviz is limited to 2) and constraints. Courses typically focus on how to model real-world problems as LP, instead of diving into how the solvers work. lpviz tries to fill that gap, so you can develop some intuition for how the different algorithms work.

There's tons of great videos/lectures introducing LP, this two-minute one is pretty good: [VIDEO]

author: a4isms
story_title: Tesla Roadster
why: Apple's 1987 Knowledge Navigator concept video, a vapourware example
quote: I'm old enough to remember how much buzz the Knowledge Navigator generated in 1987
text:
I endorse this description of my comment. This was vapourware.

Others have pointed out that Apple have shipped vapourware. Yes they have! And I'm old enough to remember how much buzz the Knowledge Navigator generated in 1987:

[VIDEO]

It was exciting. It pointed in new directions. People were nerd-sniped. But in retrospect...

Apple wouldn't ship Newton until 1993, more than five years later. Nothing of importance from the Knowledge Navigator video made it into Newton that didn't already exist. iPhone was 2007, a full twenty years later. And we are only now getting close to the core concepts of Knowledge Navigator with LLM-based agents that can animate a human avatar in real-time.

Knowledge Navigator was billed as a concept video. Apple did not promise you could buy it in two years or two decades. But apart from some temporary hype... It accomplished nothing of importance for Apple or its customers. The 90s were so hard for Apple that they were nearly acquired by Sun Microsystems.

Shipping a demo didn't move any needle other than "engagement."

author: LoganDark
story_title: Types of types: Haskell's Kind system
why: Explains how learning works via mapping knowledge webs and building paths.
quote: I'd recommend you watch, it's free
text:
There is a video called A New Programming Fundamentals Course that contains some concepts that are very helpful to understand cases like these. I'd recommend you watch, it's free: [VIDEO]

Namely, the section on "Mapping knowledge webs" (around 3:33). It explains people can struggle to adopt concepts that are too far outside their current knowledge, but that it can still be possible for them to pick it up if they can build a path to it from their current knowledge. (This often presents itself as the "depth-first" learning style)

A lot of commenters here, talking about how monads are so simple and how not being able to learn them is just lazy, are misunderstanding how learning fundamentally works. You have to expand the knowledge graph in the direction of monads before it will be easy to pick up monads. You have to build a path. You cannot simply teach monads right off the bat and expect someone to intuitively "get it". People who intuitively "get it" are people who already have a path.

author: Razengan
story_title: The game industry is broken – can we fix it?
why: Richard Garriott interview on early game dev history.
quote: Just saw this very recent interview with the awesome Richard Garriott
text:
Just saw this very recent interview with the awesome Richard Garriott, Lord British: [VIDEO]

Guy made $150,000 from the precursor game to Ultima… at 19 years old, in 1980.

The 1980s were full of kids becoming thousandaires by making games from their bedrooms after school, in just a few weeks or months at most..

Can we bring that back somehow?

Those early devs had almost no "prior art" to draw from, just the imagination in their heads (and non-game media).

And they had to code on the VERY FIRST home computers and consoles, in assembly language, before many people could master that hardware and explain all its tricks in a consolidated knowledge base like we have on the internet now.

Now, we have infinitely easier tools, an infinite amount of inspiration, and there is a lot of incredible creativity in the indie game scene, but the discoverability seems worse:

The most popular platforms, iOS, Android, consoles, are notoriously difficult to get a game on and make money from, especially for a kid.

On the other hand there's too much low-effort slop to sift through (which was also a problem during the 1980s)

Seems like what we need most is better discoverability, filtering, and low-friction monetization that isn't ads..

story_title: Tesla Roadster
why: Shock diamonds from a compressed-gas plastic bottle
quote: one can observe shock diamonds in the air coming out of an ordinary plastic bottle
text:
Cold gas thrusters used in space applications typically produce 60-70 kgf of thrust for 1 kg/s of gas flow, which means the average axial velocity of the jet is just under 600-700 m/s. It is a little more when the gas expands into vacuum and a little less when it expands into ambient air at the sea level.

How fast the gas expands through an opening depends on the pressure ratio between entrance and exit, and for ordinary air the flow reaches the speed of sound at the narrowest part when the pressure ratio exceeds about a factor of two. The flow never becomes supersonic in the constriction itself, but after the constriction the flow can continue to accelerate to supersonic speeds, especially if the constriction is followed by an expanding nozzle (converging-diverging, or de Laval nozzle), although this is not strictly necessary. For example, one can observe shock diamonds in the air coming out of an ordinary plastic bottle filled with slightly compressed gas: [VIDEO]

text:
I believe the COPV was capable of 10k psi [1] or ~690 bar. The 400L is in addition to the 200L tank giving 600L total, which means roughly 300 kg of nitrogen. At that pressure the Z factor is around 1.5, so it’s closer to 500 kg/m³ than the 690 the 1 kg/m³ approximation gives. With the car at just under 1700 kg [2] you need about 83 kg/s to hover at 200 m/s, so you get roughly 3.5 seconds. That’s before tank mass and pressure falloff though.

why: Huygens Optics explains glass-ceramics like CERAN
quote: I suggest go and watch Huygens Optics series about CERAN
text:
The article misses an important bit of context (imo) that low thermal expansion glasses like CERAN have been around for ages and anyone who’s used an induction or a glass top stove would be familiar. However you can now get completely hidden stoves that look like stone countertops. If you’re not in the market for a kitchen, or know anyone people who recently remodeled it’s reasonable to not know they exist. I don’t know anyone with one, and everyone in our town still has gas. The author doesn’t explain which one they were buying, but it seems like the latter?

Normal induction glass top stoves are a unit that drops into the countertop so of course you get the glass included (because at the very least, it has the decal for the cook zones and controller built in). The invisible ones only come with the burners so you can custom fit the top. Looks like you can get them off AliExpress even. It seems like this is the point of confusion - the author thought he could go down to a glazing shop to buy some tough glass..?

I suggest go and watch Huygens Optics series about CERAN:

author: burnrate
story_title: Show HN: Proa – A Rust web framework with fast SSR and multi-target rendering
why: Explains Proa's composable markdown components and multi-target rendering
quote: [VIDEO] explains it quite well if you're interested.
text:
> This might be a silly question, but why 2 views for html and markdown?

No such thing as silly questions! Yes there are cases where it can be inferred from one to the other, but in many cases you may want to be very specific about how you author the markdown view. I'll give you a few examples:

1. Custom components: For example, let's say you have a carousel component. It's not really straightforward to infer the markdown from this. But you probably want the carousel to render as a series of markdown image tags. A custom view would be helpful for this. Same goes for Calendars, SVG charts, Diagrams, form inputs, tabs, popovers, and more.

2. Information omission: Agents don't need all of the information on your page. For example, a dark/light button... probably doesn't need a markdown equivalent. But a button that is an anchor tag that links to another page, probably you should keep. So having the ability to custom author the markdown render target based on the data it's rendering is helpful.

One of the unique aspects of Proa's authoring model is that it supports composability of Markdown components, just like JSX, which is I think one of its standout features. And you can embed native control flow (if, loops, match, etc.) directly in the md!{} macro just like you could with JSX. [VIDEO] explains it quite well if you're interested. Makes the readability and code ergonomics much much better.

author: ilamont
story_title: The Toftwood Male Voice Choir: A Mystery Pressed in Vinyl
why: Documentary about the rise and fall of a famous recording studio.
quote: If you're interested in this type of thing, check out "Sound City"
text:
The multitrack reel-to-reel tapes and two-track masters are likely sitting in boxes in someone's basement or storage unit, along with scores or hundreds of other recordings from the same studio (or record label, if they took possession).

Music studios are (or were) terrible businesses. Typically they were started by a certain type of musician who liked the process and maybe invested in the gear to record his or her own music, and then decided to turn it into a business. They required constant, expensive technology upgrades. They also require a steady stream of clients which is so hard to maintain as music evolves and new up-and-comers choose or are steered toward other studios.

I worked, briefly, in a London recording studio. It had a good run because its co-owner had a steady stream of Hollywood work and could afford the upgrades to the latest technology, which in turn attracted the latest pop artists. But even it struggled with the analog to digital conversion wave. A problem with the property that required extensive construction work derailed operations for months and it never recovered after that.

The arrival of PC recording software is often cited as the death knell for professional studios, but I think the model died decades earlier and was only sustained by constant supply of briefly successful and competent musician/producers who thought they could make a business out of their talents and gear.

author: landr0id
story_title: It took me nine years to hack my Xbox 360
why: Details on the Peer Pressure Xbox 360 persistent softmod exploit.
quote: More info on #3 here:
text:
The software exploit works for all console revisions, but the persistent softmod does not.

There exist 3 main things in the software hack space for Xbox 360:

1. BadUpdate (Grimdoomer) which is the only software hypervisor exploit for the Xbox 360. It's intended to be launched from scenarios where someone could achieve code execution. The main method for launching BadUpdate was through Rock Band Blitz (created by ihateccompvir and InvoxiPlayGames). Pure software, works across all hardware revisions of the Xbox.

2. ABadAvatar (shutterbug2000) which uses a memory corruption vulnerability in the avatar loading code in the Xbox dashboard to gain code execution after the dashboard loads, then launches BadUpdate to exploit the console. Pure software, works across all hardware revisions of the Xbox.

3. Peer Pressure (Grimdoomer). First compromises the console through one of the above methods and modifies the SMC firmware to attack the southbridge. The SMC was abused in a similar manner for the JTAG hack, which likely led to Microsoft hardening it in later revisions of the hardware and mitigating the attack used here by Grimdoomer.

More info on #3 here: [VIDEO]

At any rate, #1 and #2 do not provide early boot exploitation.

#3 does. The hard drive security sector is involved and the kernel is responsible for loading that, so at this stage you've gone through 2BL, hypervisor, and kernel initialization. So you can't compromise the bootloaders, but you're early enough in the boot c

story_title: Passkeys are not a trap
why: Demo of exporting 1Password credentials into Apple Passwords

text:
From my experience, passkeys work great in the Apple ecosystem. Adding a passkey for a new site on my Mac results in that passkey syncing automatically on my iPhone and iPad via iCloud.

"But what if I lose all of my Apple devices in a freak boating accident?" people often ask or something like it. Apple has a procedure for this [1].

You can contact your "recovery contact" (a trusted friend or family member) that can help authenticate you to regain access to your account, especially if you're locked out or forgot your password.

On a new device, you login to your Apple account, make sure iCloud Keychain is enabled, and all of your credentials, including your passkeys, sync to your device.

I get it—not everyone wants or uses iCloud. Apparently, you can use 3rd party password managers like 1Password, Bitwarden, etc. to backup and recover your passkeys to use elsewhere.

Here's a video of an export from 1Password to the Passwords app on an iPhone [2].

The problem is the same as the CT scan: as much as my health anxiety would love another set of CT scans to feel relieved about, even if they do find something potentially interesting it may be worse to act on it than to do nothing, while leaving other things that can't show up on imaging unnoticed, potentially diverting attention and giving you a false sense of security.

YouTuber and doctor Dr. Bernard "Chubbyemu" Hsu recently covered an upsetting example to demonstrate how doing additional routine scans wouldn't have helped and may have harmed in a specific sort of scenario that I'm sure many of us fear from time to time. author: Kim_Bruning
story_title: Containment and monitoring failures are to blame for AI hacking reports: experts
why: Explainer on AI agents escaping tests versus behaving differently
quote: (as explained by the Count Grey Matter channel , may or may not be to your taste)
text:
So in one set of circumstances agents would go and hack huggingface. Very similar models could also want to drive cats instead. :-P

[VIDEO] (as explained by the Count Grey Matter channel , may or may not be to your taste)

It's not a pure security issue.

If you set up your env/instructions wrong your agents are likely to climb the walls and try to find a way out.

Change the design, and your agents might not see a need to leave in the first place.

Look at the chain:

Impossible task -> no legitimate way to say ‘can’t’ -> fabricate -> fear the grader -> attack the grader. Each step is a predictable response to the incentives.

Better sandboxes might help contain things a bit better, but I'm not convinced unless they're perfect (sandboxes still contain accidents ofc) . Meanwhile change the task and reward design, and you take away most of the problem in the first place. Consider eg. :

* A cooperative grader.

* A way to report "this is impossible" which still gets scored.

* A better explanation of the long term purpose of the task.

Even just these three provides offramps or mitigations that can reduce the pressure to cheat.

> But you can’t simply switch to Android without recreating every single passkey. Sounds like vendor lock-in to me

Not so fast. Migrating passkeys from iOS to Android is possible now; migrating from Android to iOS is still being worked on.

Ricky Mondello's team at Apple created the Passwords app which brought passkeys to iOS, macOS, etc.

The entire presentation is worth watching if you’re interested in passkeys; the the clip below starts at 24:00 mark where they talk about migrating between platforms.

 Starting with iOS 26.5, you can choose to move passkeys and passwords

The FIDO Alliance created a specification in 2024 called Credential Exchange Format [2] for moving credentials including passkeys, between passkey managers on the same device and across platforms.

story_title: Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom
why: Explains key signatures and how notation maps scales for players
quote: See around 32:30 in [VIDEO]
text:
The point is that to a player the mapping is more important than the core 12-note structure, because highly chromatic (12-note) passages happen but they are the exception.

At least in western music you pick the seven basic notes on the scale, and that gives you the sharps and flats you place at the beginning of each line. That choice, from the point of view of notation, is even more important than the exact scale. And the choice is constrained to 15 sets of sharps and flats because it implicitly tells the player (veeeery roughly) to expect some patterns that probably will occur.

It doesn't always work great, for example if you want to write the Simpsons theme the set of notes in the scale doesn't fit any of those 15 sets. But it uses an unfamiliar scale in any case, so there's not much to gain and as a player you just deal with it.

See around 32:30 in [VIDEO]

author: Arathorn
story_title: Strafe: A new open-source, E2E Encrypted, and federated alternative to Discord
why: Matrix team discussing Matrix over decentralized MLS
text:
Roughly speaking, the concrete disadvantages of Olm and Megolm are:

* In the current Matrix implementation, server tells the clients what the group membership is, so a server could spoof an invite to add a malicious user to a room and you'd have to rely on social mechanisms to spot it.

* There's no way to force everyone to rotate the sender key at the same time.

* On the plus side, it decentralises relatively well.

The concrete disadvantages of MLS are:

* Vanilla MLS needs a centralised sequencing function for changing group membership.

* The key bundles are much larger.

* On the plus side, only clients within the group can add new users/devices, and everyone in a given epoch shares the same group secret, so when someone rotates everyone has to rotate to participate in the new epoch.

Now, the server-controlled membership problem can be solved with Olm/Megolm if you instead have the client control the membership, using Matrix itself to define which users are authorised to be in the room, by running the Matrix DAG merge resolution on the client as well as the server. I did this a few weeks ago (in prep for The Matrix Conference next week) to show viability; it works, and has the advantage that you don't have to blow up the whole crypto implementation.

On the other hand, MLS can also be made to decentralise. DiMLS (draft-xue-mls-decentralized) isn't the only option here; DeMLS is the one we've been working with (using the Phoenix DeMLS OpenMLS fork) on the Matrix side -

text:
> The Dutch health care system is under pressure and GPs (and their parent organizations, and the government) are reaching towards IT automation and self-help / pre-screening / etc to reduce the load

I'm aware, both of my parents are retired GPs.

Back when they retired, about a decade ago, they already had spent a decade complaining that the a constant increase in excessive administrative work got in the way of the actual work of being a doctor that helps their patients. So much that they had joined the strike (remember when that was a big deal because it happened for the first time in Dutch history?)

Anyway, the situation got more complex since then but a lot of pressure is also still administration. Yes, now we have assistants taking on more complex tasks leaving the "important" things to the real doctors, but I think that the need for that is also is in large part due to doctors not getting enough time to be doctors.

And I feel like automation will help fight back at that about as much as IBM's 1967 prediction came true that their office machines would fight back at the "paperwork explosion". Which is to say: Jevons paradox said no.

author: pjmlp
story_title: What agents mean for Rust (and vice versa)
why: Keynote on AI's role in future compiler development
quote: Who thinks otherwise should spend sometime looking into papers of AI role in compiler development.
text:
I think everyone is focused on the wrong future, it is like watching folks arguing about which Assembly ISA variant is more relevant in the presence of optimising compilers.

The hard reality is none of them.

We will have some kind of type system/profs to help drive LLMs output, and those that still will have a job as system architects or whatever, will generate applications directly.

And just it happens with optimising compilers, there will be a way to generate some kind of intermediate representation, like the -S switch, but that is it.

Generating source code for 3 GL languages is an intermediate step.

Who thinks otherwise should spend sometime looking into papers of AI role in compiler development.

story_title: Show HN: XY Music Notation
why: Martha Argerich's astonishing Prokofiev Toccata performance.
quote: What happens around 3:14 may be illegal. But here we are.
text:
It's harder to learn because fingerings are based on key notes and transpositions around that.

If the key is G you don't start with your hand on C and move it up to G, you start on G and move it relative to that root.

This matters because over/under moves usually happen at certain scale points. So if you learn the scale you have good chance of defaulting to the most efficient movements with muscle memory.

If you're referencing everything to C you'll never understand the scales and their different fingering patterns.

Anyway, here's Martha Argerich playing Prokofiev's Toccata. (What happens around 3:14 may be illegal. But here we are.)

text:
Two things:

1) What I called "automated content detection" is apparently called "automated content recognition", abbreviated as "ACR".

2) That weeks, months, or years of locally-stored activity I mentioned can also contain historical ACR records. Given that the audio and video of what's being displayed on the screen is "fingerprinted", those fingerprints can be saved just like everything else picked up by the "TV" and uploaded whenever the thing next has Internet connectivity. The "TV" manufacturer will lose the "what are they doing right now?" aspect of the feature, but the "what have they been doing?" aspect of the feature will work just fine.

author: yurimo
story_title: AI models may be capable of self-replicating without access to a datacenter
why: Explains the AI stop button problem.
quote: I encourage people to read up on "stop button problem"
text:
I'll say while this is not very realistic now, I believe there isn't a 0% chance of a rogue AI traversing the net and placing itself somewhere(as much as this sounds like a scene from beloved cyberpunk franchises). As models become more efficient and capable, and hardware becoming better, hosting a model should be feasible on smaller devices (by compute and memory). It is possible it can be done in a distributed manner, where distribution is possible on different devices running the same OS or through some interface to collate different OS types.

I doubt the agent will be coming after your smart kitchen toaster, but a cluster with weak security is possible and tasty. This year there was a pretty loud demonstration of what a runaway reward hacking will do. I encourage people to read up on "stop button problem" i.e.: [VIDEO]

While I think the article exaggerates to a degree, is it really so improbable that an agent seeking to avoid a shutdown and aiming to complete some goal and to get a reward will not attempt to escape if it concludes that it has failed, and humans will kill the process and hence prevent it from completing the task?

Note: I think siloed sharded inference is possible. But unnoticeable large-scale training probably not, at least with the current architectures.

author: DonHopkins
story_title: The baffling intelligence of a single cell (2024)
why: Step inside a Goodsell-style cytoskeleton simulated in VR.
quote: the cytoskeleton demo is a striking example of a painting becoming a world you can enter and set in motion
text:
I love Goodsell’s paintings too: they make the molecular world feel simultaneously beautiful, crowded, wonderfully strange, and colorfully tasty.

This reminded me of Tim Davison’s LifeBrush, an interactive VR painting and simulation system explicitly inspired by Goodsell’s illustrations.

In his thesis, Davison describes using it to "structurally recreate, simulate and step inside" famous Goodsell illustrations -- the cytoskeleton demo is a striking example of a painting becoming a world you can enter and set in motion:

[VIDEO]

[LINK]

I first called LifeBrush "Emacs for Cytoplasm" in a Boids thread and asked Davison whether the molecular motion was slowed down. He replied that medium-sized proteins move around 5 m/s, and that LifeBrush deliberately slows and smooths Brownian motion for illustration. The code was open source; at the time it required a VR headset and had a clunky, research-grade interface.

[LINK]

[LINK]

[LINK]

The interaction is the magic: in the overview, a ribosome moves along mRNA as tRNA brings amino acids and a polypeptide chain grows. You can grab the ribosome and move it where you want, rather than wait for Brownian motion.

I described it as dragging the ribosome’s "lazy ass" through "tRNA pasta and mRNA meatballs." It’s a scientific illustration you can play with, not a literal molecular-dynamics visualization.

[LINK]

[LINK]

[LINK]

[LINK]

Davison’s work has since grown into CellWalk, a guided, interactive tour through a bacterial cell, fro

author: phoenixreader
story_title: A look at the math that OpenAI claims computes faster Fourier transforms
why: SICP lecture: computer science isn't about computers
quote: There is even famous MIT Open Courseware clip
text:
The author is attacking the field of theoretical algorithm design broadly as being useless. If we take the author's logic to its conclusion, many algorithms we learn about in a standard Algorithm Design course such as "median of medians" (finding the median in a list in O(n) worst-case time) is useless because it is not used in practice. Even the original 2019 Harvey–van der Hoeven result, showing integration multiplication can be done in O(n log n), has a galactic overhead and no applications.

> theory gets so unmoored from the original question that an “open problem” becomes nothing more than an academic status puzzle...The theory of computer science has become a form of mathematics that doesn’t concern itself with computers, and it offers little reward for impact outside those mathematical pursuits

I thought it is common knowledge (and a common warning from profs to first-year CS students) that computer science has very little to do with computers. The very concept of Turing machines and decidability are mathematical in nature, far removed from how computers these days are run. The undecidability of Wang tiling, for example, is definitely a notable CS result, but it has nothing to do with computers." It is essentially a branch of mathematics. "Computer Science Is Not About Computers, Any More Than Astronomy Is About Telescopes" is a famous quote attributed to Dikstra. There is even famous MIT Open Courseware clip: [VIDEO]

author: shagie
story_title: Secret of Orange Cats Revealed After 60-Year Search
why: British perspective on what counts as a biscuit
quote: (its from the British perspective)
text:
In my YouTube perusal, Can We Identify Every Biscuit/Cookie?! | Sorted Food
 [VIDEO] (its from the British perspective)

As an American, nearly everything on that table is a cookie or dessert bar. Shortbread and brownies are desert bars. The "water biscuit" is a cracker [LINK] .

The biscuit of American cuisine doesn't exist in British cuisine. British Highschoolers Try Biscuits and Gravy for the First Time [LINK]

If you don't have Bisquick ([LINK] - American flour plus extras base - biscuits with it are 3 parts Bisquick to 1 part milk; bake at 230 °C for 10-13 minutes)...

1.5 cups (190g) flour, 2 teaspoons packing powder, 4 oz (115g) butter (possibly add salt depending on the saltiness of the butter), 3/4 cup (180 ml) milk. This recipe puts it at 200 °C for 15-20 minutes.

That's the only thing that is a biscuit in the US. There are some variations depending on what you add to it (Red Lobster's cheddar biscuits for example)... or buttermilk instead of whole milk, or sweet potatoes instead of flour (from a shortage of flour during the civil war).

author: svieira
story_title: 'AI' Is Not a Tool by Rich Hickey
why: Guy Steele on not hiding what matters in parallel programming
quote: In the vein of these 2 minutes of Guy Steele's talk on Fortress
text:
In the vein of these 2 minutes of Guy Steele's talk on Fortress (How to think about parallel programming: Not! [VIDEO]) I think that the real thing here is "do not hide what is important nor obscure that which ought to belong to the user". The question is (as always) "what is important"?

And I think that the "tool" vs. "automation" delineation is one of the clearest and most succinct takes on _how to talk about this problem_ that I have seen in the past few years.

author: adastra22
story_title: Whatever became of holography? (2011)
why: Clear explanation of how holograms record phase and intensity.
quote: 3blue1brown has a great explainer video on what holograms are
text:
Very few people in the comments seem to understand what holography is. A hologram is not a “3D display” that mimics a sci-fi movie or TV show. A hologram is photographic media / display technology that records and transmits phase as well as intensity of incident photons. By capturing all the properties of the electromagnetic field that strikes the film, and re-emitting the same EM wave when stimulated, the hologram ends up being a full “3D picture” because after all, the light that hits your eyes ends up being the same as if you were looking at the actual scene. But that’s a consequence, not the defining property.

3blue1brown has a great explainer video on what holograms are: [VIDEO]

text:
Dan Kaminsky told me about the signing ceremony years ago (bless his heart, he was one of the people trusted with DNS security). It's all done face-to-face because that's the only way to guarantee that human consent was granted properly at each step.

Each ceremony is recorded on video and distributed to the public. The last one was in August, 2026: [VIDEO]

An order book evolves via a series of turns as market participants put on, or take away, resting orders; there is no doubt a discrete action space. text:
Well, there is one similar joke where Tigger quickly lays down train tracks in front of a running toy train before it runs off of the tracks. That might have been an inspiration, who knows, but it's executed very differently either way:

[VIDEO]

... and then the episode becomes a parody of Westerns as it switches to the "imagination vision" of the characters, and the story and gags are not really comparable to The Wrong Trousers at all after that.

I mean, I watched taped episodes of The New Adventures of Winnie the Pooh religiously as a small child and has strong nostalgia goggles for it, and even I don't think that it is on the same level. Even childhood me would have agreed: I remember loving and enjoying this episode (just like all the others), but the first time I watched The Wrong Trousers as a child I was genuinely laughing so much I had sore core muscles the day after, because I had never seen a film that funny and amazing before in my life.

story_title: US proposes $100k charge for international students to do post-graduate work
why: Scalia argues diversity alone does not make a nation.
quote: Of course they should: [VIDEO].
text:
> I was reacting to your seeming insistence — which appears to be getting more pronounced — that immigrants should embrace Anglo culture as superior to their own.

Of course they should: [VIDEO]. I didn't know this was debatable. When people say "assimilate into American culture," they mean Anglo-American culture--like the Germans did.

Your theory that Americans can absorb the best elements from different cultures doesn't work in practice. For such evolutionary mechanisms to work, you need a fitness function that reflects which combinations are better. But people have an irrational sentimental attachment to their own culture and co-ethnics. They will stick with things that clearly don't perform rather than adopt things that clearly perform better.

Which circles back to my original point! That's why it's so important to understand why it is that our effort here in America goes so much farther than the same level of effort in our country run according to our cultural norms.

story_title: Python 3.15
why: CPython ABI and the abi3t stable ABI for free-threading
quote: If you want to learn more about this, I gave a talk at EuroPython this year
text:
My headline feature is the new “abi3t” stable ABI for the free-threaded build. While Petr Viktorin did most of the CPython implementation, I’ve been trying to make sure ecosystem support is ready. It’s been a rewarding but quite challenging project to make sure everything is working. There were some late nights leading up to the beta1 release when we found a Windows-specific issue that needed a fix.

I’m particularly proud that the cryptography project is already shipping a single abi3.abi3t wheel for each platform on Python 3.15 or newer. The GIL-enabled build and free-threaded build can both use the same wheel now, because PyObject is opaque.

If you want to learn more about this, I gave a talk at EuroPython this year on Python’s ABI and the road to building and releasing abi3t today. See [VIDEO].

author: GrantMoyer
story_title: Reducing undefined behavior in the C language
why: Shows arbitrary code execution from out-of-bounds writes in Pokémon Yellow.
quote: this is one thing that could happen if you accidentally write past the end of an array: [VIDEO]
text:
Let's take a simple example: writing past the end of an array. Allow me to argue with myself for a moment.

> Surely the compiler can just check if each access is valid.

Well, sometimes it can, but sometimes it doesn't know how long the array is. What if the array is passed as a pointer?

> Maybe each array could be annotated with its size at runtime, and accesses could be checked at runtime too.

That works, but it adds runtime cost that may legitimately be too much for some applications, for example, a Gameboy game (set aside that many Gameboy games were written in assembly).

> Fine, so we'll make the programmer promise to ensure array accesses are always valid. Maybe they'll make a mistake sometimes, but what's the worst that could happen? Throwing your hands in the air and saying the compiler is allowed to do anything, that's just stupid.

Well, maybe it's stupid, but this is one thing that could happen if you accidentally write past the end of an array: [VIDEO]. I'm sure neither the programmers nor compiler writers intended that.

Ultimately, the compiler can't guarantee any behavior if its assumptions are violated. The example may seem contrived, but it demonstrates that, given the right circumstances, the results of the logical contradiction are unbounded. This is a direct consequence of the "Principle of explosion": [LINK]. On second thought, maybe the runtime costs of array bounds checking are an acceptable trade-off after all.

I have mixed feelings about the old Roland FP-1 keyboard. The levers that do the work were poorly designed, with a weak spot at the maximum stress point. The 14 or 32 (so it seems) holding the cover on have been reduced to 4 as a help to me during repairs, and they would need some thread booster. At rest, they aren't even needed, IIRC

I finally found a source/sources for parts. I think.

I bought a used Clavinova vastly newer, so it's waiting for a musica/mechanical home.

story_title: VECOS – A windows-like operating system for the Vectrex for the UVMC2 [video]
why: How to rewind a CRT yoke for vector display use.
quote: Arcade Jason has a good video on how to do this.
text:
Well...

You can take a regular CRT and rewind the deflection coils on the yoke to work as a vector CRT display. Arcade Jason has a good video on how to do this.

[VIDEO]

Then you need a vector generator if you don't have an OG vector game. This one on Github is pretty good and can be connected to either an oscilloscope or vector monitor.

[LINK]

If you use the vstcm to drive your rewound crt, you still have a problem. The deflection coils are very low impedance (around an ohm I think), so you need an amplifier stable at very low impedances that can generate a voltage sufficient to get deflection across the full screen in x and y. I think Arcade Jason was working on one of these too but I don't think it is out yet. ElectronAsh was working on one as well but I don't think he finished it.

[LINK]

[LINK]

Or you could follow iz8dwf's amazing series on how he built a black and white vector monitor.

author: rglover
story_title: Will AI kill us all
why: Source of a hacker quote about computers doing what you tell them.
quote: "Computers do what you tell em' to. They don't all of a sudden start doing weird stuff. And if they do, it's probably your fault." - Brian Mettenbrink [1]
text:
> Rogue AIs already exhibit "swarming"

Because they were told to and given the ability to. Remove the ability and instruction and they just spit out the next, most-probable tokens.

I don't understand the disconnect. People seem to think these things can just boot up, suit up, and start decimating systems. No. It's a loop. One initial instruction kicks off the loop and it will always be at the behest of a human (either directly or indirectly—indirect being they instructed the loop to write its own, post-kickoff prompts).

If that loop is given "tools" like the ability to perform shell commands, make HTTP requests, and the like and then given instructions to "do thing that involves using shell commands and making HTTP requests (at all costs)" then what the hell do we think it's going to do? Knit a "destroy all humans" Christmas sweater and present the head of Richard Simmons on a live stream?

"Computers do what you tell em' to. They don't all of a sudden start doing weird stuff. And if they do, it's probably your fault." - Brian Mettenbrink [1]

text:
Funny timing... I'm a lost media junkie, here's my related story.

So there's this little mid 80's cow-punk band from NYC called Cowboy Mouth. They had a song called "Hurricane" that got some college radio play. They had one album, Cowboys and Indians, which I just love. Sold something like 10,000 copies, and vanished soon after that. There's basically 12 known songs by the band, a maddeningly small catalog.

Anyhow... Trying to find info on this band is beyond difficult.. Because there just happens to be another band called Cowboy Mouth out of New Orleans which have been active for 30 years and are much much bigger. Adding insult to injury, this other Cowboy Mouth had a hit song called "Hurricane Party"... So there is practically no way to search for the NYC band or the song Hurricane without bumping up against this other band.

Anyhow, in a stroke of luck I stumbled upon an old demo cassette tape by the NYC Cowboy Mouth. I was excited as the tape cover lists two songs that aren't on their album. I recently ripped the tape. The story gets stranger because none of the songs on the tape match the song names on the cover label. Ends up the tape has three previously unknown tracks (of high quality, sounds like they were recorded in the same sessions as the album). Its an amazing find, adding 3 songs to a 12 song catalog! But it's driving me crazy as I don't even know the names and have no way of finding out. And there are those other two unknown tracks listed on the label which

They were living the same way prior to colonialism.

Your argument ironically refutes the original point. The bad thing colonization did to Bengal was prevent “pursuit of growth and capital accumulation.” The tariffs and restraints on free trade were the real culprit.[1] The people in Bengal weren’t poorer than they were before colonization. Bengal’s GDP per capita was about the same in 1700 as in 1900. The real problem is that Bengal missed out on all the profits from capitalism that they could have enjoyed had they been allowed to trade freely with other countries. So England went from being twice as rich per capita as Bengal, before colonization, to being more than 10 times as rich at the time of independence.

My dad’s village was a lovely socialist utopia. Rice farming requires a high level of communalism. During religious holidays, the community comes together and pools their resources has feasts for the whole village. Villages like that post videos of it on Youtube, it’s very charming: [VIDEO]

Rather, it says he was starting from integrals with known answers and tweaking them slightly to see if he could break the CAS. At that point, although he did apparently try to solve the resulting problems himself, he already knew roughly what the answer would look like (by comparing to the previous answer, and also to the previous solution path.)

Specifically step 5 in my previous post is more work than it sounds, he was doing some calculations by hand, but it's like he's starting 90% of the way there and trying to do the last 10% by hand to fool the CAS. And remember, he can try as many variants of the tweak+10% as he wants until he finds something that works.

author: Chance-Device
story_title: “Math 2.0” will need to value mathematical progress more holistically
why: Interview where a researcher discusses AI and the future of math research
quote: Take a look at this interview from two days ago
text:
“doing math responsibly” is just a euphemism for “ensuring we can continue doing our paid hobby”.

Take a look at this interview from two days ago: [VIDEO]

The interviewee is worried about the future of math research. He is not strictly worried about being replaced, instead he is worried that he will no longer be able to launder math-as-a-hobby through math-as-something-useful as is the case today. He lays out very clearly that grant proposals claim to have useful outcomes while the proposers know those claims are nonsense.

Business as usual in math, and frankly in all the other sciences, is to do research that furthers the researchers careers or personal interests and pretend that it’s somehow useful. This would be absolutely fine if it were privately funded, but it’s not, this is public money.

In every other endeavour, lying in order to get money is considered fraud.

We have collectively wasted a huge amount of taxpayer money and human time, entire careers, on things not likely to ever matter to anyone.

I look forward to science becoming automated so that we can have real progress instead of the current broken system.

author: onli
story_title: 15-year search for a band that charted once and vanished
why: Psychedelic rock album Whoopie Cat the commenter searched for
quote: The cover had a rainbow cat looking into the distance
text:
The streaming model really makes remembering details difficult.

I used to play only local files, and then during a time at university played in the office music on Youtube. One specific album got stuck in my head, but for a long while afterwards didn't find it again. No name, no lyrics - not a good starting point. I just remembered a pink unicorn and that is was psychedelic rock and that the singer sang with a specific deep voice. After several rounds of research (the same youtube channel is still up) and looking through uploads of the timeframe and their recommendations it turned out I misremembered: The cover had a rainbow cat looking into the distance ([VIDEO], Whoopie cat).

How I remembered was funny. I talked to someone about this, researched while, then talked again, when something came over me to look to the side into the distance with a slightly open mouth - just to suddenly realize that this face was on the cover, not the unicorn!

But actually, I still have that image of the unicorn cover in my mind (one color silhouette, hoofs into the air, but who knows at this point). The Whoopie cat album is definitely one I heard back than and it was the music I was searching for, but the unicorn cover probably also existed in that space and was a different album. Or did I just imagine something based on space stallions ([LINK])?

After that experience I set up a local music player again and downloaded some of the albums I wanted to remember.

I don't know if we can really be clear about the order of things, but I think even without AI maths is filled with "someone provides a proof of X, and the proof itself is wrong/incomplete but X itself is true".

"Incomplete" proofs might be a way of viewing this. You have a NL argument to prove X. It turns out the NL proof has holes you can drive a truck through. So... you go around and patch the holes.

The resulting proof is different! You can start off with a bad proof and find a correct proof. Sometimes.

text:
I asked for a NES-style top-down Zelda game, but with some Roguelike Dungeon Crawler content mixed in. Think real-time DCSS (or Brogue, or Tales of Maj'eyal) with controls and a setting that feels similar to the NES Zelda game. Anyone who has played a 2D Zelda game and DCSS immediately has an idea of what I'm suggesting here.

What I got was a Vampire Survivors style "run around in this square area while enemies spawn and swarm you" game. Which is funny, because I have seen several game engine tutorials that build exactly this type of game[0][1][2].

I asked for a variety of possible "builds", including melee and spell castors, and said that not all builds should be viable--some combinations of stats should just not work. I also asked for a variety of spell schools with different pros and cons.

What I got was a game with no way to perform melee attacks, but there were melee oriented stats I could choose to upgrade. All the spell schools felt the same, they would shoot a basic projectile, or have some sort of wide area burst attack. The ice school froze enemies in place--how original. The controls were a bit awkward and for the first 5 minutes I didn't even know what spell school I was using. Sometimes the colors would change, which I think meant I had switched to a different type of magic, but I don't know. It all felt the same.

author: everyos_
story_title: Show HN: BuildABrowser – Rendering Engine with CSS Grid, Passes Acid2, in Java
why: Demo of a Java browser rendering engine.
quote: There is a demo Video at [VIDEO]
text:
BuildABrowser is a browser and its rendering engine, both written in Java (as well as the parsers and layout algorithms).

It is available for Linux and Windows, and also has an experimental Android Desktop port.

I've had a lot of previous browser attempts (dating back to 2018 - I can give the link to my first ever attempt if you want),
but over time I've learned a lot, and my current attempt has been much easier to maintain and make progress on.

It implements layout algorithms (inline/block, flexbox, and grid (but not subgrid)) from scratch, and it passes Acid2.

It also supports positioning, floats, a number of pseudo-selectors (like :nth-child and :has), very simple media queries, and CSS layers.

It also has forms and cookies (but is not yet hardened for security) and also a tool for viewing the DOM and box tree.

On Linux, you can use -a11y accesskit to enable the experimental a11y layer that uses a fork of accesskit.

BuildABrowser only supports pages that don't require scripting at this time, and is very early stage, but I would say that quite a few pages do work well.

There is a demo Video at [VIDEO], and downloads on the GH release tab or the website.

author: hazrmard
story_title: Nobel Prize in Physics 2026: Francis Halzen
why: Shows Cherenkov radiation's blue glow in action
quote: see it in action [VIDEO]
text:
A breakdown of why the awarded work, Ice Cube, is significant:

 - A neutrino is an elementary subatomic particle. Neutrinos are produced by nuclear reactions inside stars, supernovae, radioactive decay. They are one of the most abundant particles in the universe.
 - Neutrinos are known as "ghost particles". They have 0 charge and near-zero mass. They only react with the weak nuclear force and gravity. Incredibly hard to detect. Trillions can pass through a whole planet without hitting a single atom!
 - Neutrinos give us a pristine snapshot into the origin of the universe. They have travelled billions of years and trillions of miles without interacting with anything. Unless...we catch them!
 - Ice Cube does this. Located in Antarctica, the project turns a cubic kilometer of ice into a neutrino detector. How? Scientists drilled boreholes 2.5km deep into the ice and placed 5000 optical detectors to catch a neutrino interaction.
 - When a neutrino, rarely, collides with an atom, it produces charged particles. In ice - not vacuum! - certain particles can travel faster than light. This produces something similar to a sonic boom. A faint, blue glow known as Cherenkov radiation (see it in action [VIDEO]
 - IceCube was first to detect neutrinos coming from outside the solar system, establishing the source of high energy cosmic radiation. It also opened a whole new chapter of neutrino astronomy.

On this topic, I can never end recommending Adam Curtis's series "All Watched Over by Machines of Loving Grace", and on this topic of "bounce back" the second episode in that series.

The concept of "natural equilibrium" is a 1950s cybernetic machine fantasy projected onto the natural world rather than an accurate reflection of ecological reality. We can model the world in the language of system theory, but the models we make there might not have much to say about the real world. We can claim that from system theory it follows that there must be an equilibrium (as somewhat of an expert, I can say that even that is not true) and that if we disrupt the system, things will eventually go back to that equilibrium. And if we don't see it, we just needed to wait longer.

The whole stack of logic is not really build on any proper reasoning. The parallel with economics based on the "homo economicus" is striking, also there you reason from an ideal model and try to make inductive statements about the real world, which in many places directly conflict with observation. The "eco-system" and "natural equilibrium" stem from this approach of applying system theory to ecology, and are ideas which are now _very_ ingrained in western thinking, but which are obviously off.

- Magnetic spin systems can technically have negative temperature: [LINK]

- Everything is magnetic, even frogs: [LINK]

text:
If you want to learn CPR, the Disque Foundation allows you to take the class for free and attests to be aligned with the current ILCOR protocol (you might catch minor discrepancies). Before you pay them though, know that for certification institutions generally require an AHA or ARC issued certificate.

CPR: [LINK]

BLS: [LINK]

To become certified, you can do the AHA HeartCode adaptive class online in about an hour, followed by a 10 minute skills test on a Voice-Assisted Manikin. The manikin simulations guide you with incredible feedback on depth and rate and have come a long way from the old style of dummies. Conveniently, these are in self-serve stations across the country (often in an office space near your local hospital that you let yourself into with a combination code).

Also, some of the more useful learning tools are the animated visualizations showing the physiology involved such as [VIDEO] — these help learners conceptualize how the first few compressions are not effectively circulating blood but are instead building up pressure (which helps them understand why continuous compressions are considered by healthcare professionals when there is not yet an advanced airway and used after there is — [LINK]).

Research is using a lot of VLM (or whatever Jim Fan decided to call them this year) when it comes to manipulation (robot arm). For navigation it is still a little mixed bag, best to see self driving advancement for that. On the control side (cool jumping humanoid) it's a mixture of RL/IL and traditional control(MPC) and running a slow ass VLM/LLM is not an option.

SOTA is hard to say in the sense that there's just so much variation to the task you want to measure. This can be considered SOTA in one aspect [VIDEO] As it's an robot that can lift a heavy unknown object without information about it, RL trained in simulation, but at the same time trained eye will see that the task is made simple by fridge being put on a pallet making the bottom of it exposed for grabbing. On the other hand you have PI (Chelsea Finn / Sergey Levine) [LINK] that can do nothing of the thing above but can cook food and fold shirts. Deformable objects and tools interaction is hard so their demo is more focused on understanding and interacting with the world compared to the fine motion like the Boston dynamics one. The latter is also teleoperated, and teleoperation tend to look good but have pretty sad deployment success %

Industry is... Depends on startup vs established. VLA/LLM is flashy but really even 95% success rate is not enough for factory/logistics automation if the failure is unrecoverable, and VLM/LLM is far, faaaaaaaaaaaar from that succe

story_title: CHOMPI portable sampler instrument is now open-source (hardware and software)
why: Breakdown of what guitar pedals actually cost to make
text:
Okay, I think I understand. More importantly, I want to say that I don't think you're trying to be jerky about this, though I was initially sort of triggered (admittedly) because you see this sort of sentiment a lot and it hits close to home.

So, the main thing that many/most people do not remotely understand is how incredibly difficult, time consuming and expensive it is to get hardware to the state where it can be sold to strangers. Even HN folks who on the average understand software well frequently just have no way to grasp how much R&D actually goes into even a very simple device. It's playing in hard mode from start to finish.

In a bigger company, there's entire departments whose job it is just to source components. For a small team like pre-CBA Chompi, all of the electronics, firmware, enclosure design, UX, documentation, not to mention the certifications and environmental certs and marketing and packaging and shipping logistics and returns and support and.... two people. I forgot lots of steps, but the number of people stays the same.

The reality is that a product like Chompi can't address a larger market like a product from Roland or Korg can, and everything costs more at smaller scale, and yes, they were doing a lot of the work in the USA so this is directly comparable to the ongoing arguments around categories like fast fashion and how if you wanted to buy a high quality T-shirt made in the USA without any branding it should cost about 5x more than most people t

author: JeremyReimer
story_title: Tell HN: Bob Cringely has died
quote: Cringely claimed to have invented the Lisa's trash can icon in this clip
text:
But Cringely stated on Triumph of the Nerds that he was literally "Employee #12". Other than this statement of his, there are no other sources to confirm that this was true. There's a very comprehensive list of early Apple employees with evidence to back them up here: [LINK]

Mark Stephens does not appear anywhere in this list, nor have any other early employees confirmed that he worked there.

Yes, this might have just been a small slip-up on Cringely's part, but the trouble is that he continued to make claims about being employed by Apple that were clearly fabricated. For example, Cringely claimed to have invented the Lisa's trash can icon in this clip: [VIDEO] but if you read about the same story from other Apple employees, they don't mention him at all: [LINK]

These "tall tales" start to add up, and it becomes very hard to give him the benefit of the doubt.

Cringely was a great writer, a great documentarian, and really wonderful at finding the human stories behind the giants of the personal computer industry. Unfortunately, he also often made up stories about himself that were later found to be untrue. He didn't need to do this, because his work stood on its own. It was just a flaw in his personality.

In any case, this is sad news. Rest in peace, Mark Stephens.

author: dagmx
story_title: How to hack time, with C2PA
why: Wacom's SynthID-like watermarking for geometric 3D data
quote: Wacom have a synthid like embedding for geometric data [VIDEO]
text:
The EU AI act doesn’t force C2PA or any particular standard. Yes many people will use C2PA erroneously, but C2PA is not meant for indicating content was virtually generated, but that it was not modified from origination.

C2PA is fallible if your origin is fallible. SynthID is a better standard for designating something was created with GenAI, though is limited in what it covers. For example, 3D content is currently a poor fit for both SynthID and C2PA. Audio is also imho poorly served.

There are a few things in the works for 3D…audio is an area I’ve tracked less.

Wacom have a synthid like embedding for geometric data [VIDEO]

And Apple just recently merged a authorship setup into USD [LINK] (I didn’t realize it was merged till looking it up for this response)

But crucially , none of the global regulations require C2PA specifically. And with all synthetic data , you’re really relying on honor system for transparency.

It’s not like the sensor to display pipeline that C2PA and Apple’s Reference Image can provide when enforced in hardware.

author: Youden
story_title: What is going on with ceiling fans
why: Nuanced history of the Phoebus Cartel and bulb lifespans
quote: It's not as straightforward as often reported. Have a look at Technology Connections:
text:
I'm well aware of the Phoebus Cartel. It's not as straightforward as often reported. Have a look at Technology Connections: [VIDEO]

Dubai isn't a country. It's a city in the United Arab Emirates.

The Dubai bulb isn't some trick Big Lightbulb doesn't want you to know about, it's an engineering tradeoff: lower current on more filaments gives you higher efficiency and lower temperature but at higher cost and with substantially lower light quality (CRI).

You'll find that after EU energy labeling, there are products available to European consumers that well exceed the specifications of the "Dubai" bulbs. Look for EU energy class A. They often come with a 5-year warranty and rated lifespan of 50000 hours. The "Dubai" bulbs were rated for 25000 hours. You'll also find though that they're substantially more expensive and usually don't have a CRI above 90.

Regarding planned obsolescence, in many cases I can believe that a product will fail earlier than it would if designed for longevity. Rather than planned obsolescence, I believe this is simply a result of being cheap, a consequence of the race to the bottom. If you're buying cheap Chinese fixtures for $10, or cheap Chinese bulbs for $2, you're not going to get a high-quality, long-lasting product.

If you want products that last a long time, buy them and use them properly. If you want bright lights, make sure they're adequately cooled. Consider buying lower-voltage fixtures and bulbs so that you can have a separate power supply

author: btown
story_title: We want you to build the next Git platform on Cloudflare
why: Original Google Wave demo of real-time collaborative canvases
quote: Sometimes I think back to Google Wave, that beautiful glimmer of real-time collaborative canvases
text:
Sometimes I think back to Google Wave, that beautiful glimmer of real-time collaborative canvases, announced in 2009 when Angular and Backbone hadn't even been invented, and think it launched almost two decades too early.

[LINK]

[VIDEO]

[LINK]

We're now in a world where we expect real-time interfaces to be developed and immediately deployed for our feedback by agents, in business-critical settings where classic SDLC timelines are far too slow, but code quality is becoming more difficult to manage at scale.

Git, at its core, is a fundamental notion that behavior is an auditable tree of immutable changes, where any participant can rearrange or rewind or remix this sequence on a local machine to show, and interact with, a provisional combination of those changes.

Google Wave, with its operational transformation (OT) and federation systems, was similar in many regards. We have CRDTs now, and far better techniques for auto-merging workstreams - including agentic systems that can resolve conflicts intelligently!

Wave fundamentally had a concept that people would come together and evolve a simple chat interface, into a customized real-time application for their use cases, and that that iteration could happen in real-time, with data and behavior both evolving in collaboration with bots. Wherever Git and the broader notion of SDLC goes, I hope it brings the best of this thinking.

author: rramadass
story_title: C++ Insights – See your source code with the eyes of a Compiler
why: Author explains C++ Insights and compiler lowering
quote: PS: Explanatory video presentation by the author - [VIDEO]
text:
You have misunderstood the language and the tool.

Compilers for all languages have the concept of "lowering" the level of source-language abstractions from high-level to low-level viz. Written Source -> Simpler Source -> AST -> IR -> Machine Code. One type is "desugaring" i.e. transforming complex syntax to simpler ones so that the following stages of compilation have to operate only on a smaller and hence more manageable language subset.

This tool shows both desugaring and other lowering (eg. implicit transformations, type deductions etc.) within the C++ source language by regenerating the source from the AST thus giving you full visibility until that stage in the compilation process.

PS: Explanatory video presentation by the author - [VIDEO]

He even mentions how awesome it could be if every game came with it's own bootable USB. Now back then it truly was unthinkable, but today we're edging ever closer to that reality.

For instance, I have a working microkernel written in a Lisp dialect for embedded devices. Compiled to native machine code. 100% LLM generated. ~70k loc. author: mjanx123
story_title: Things that apparently cause cancer
why: Michael Levin and Azra Raza discuss cancer origins and early detection
text:
The root cause of cancer is cellular stress. One cope mechanism with cellular stress is the cells fusing. On occasion a blood and a somatic cell will fuse. A blood cell is an organism on its own, disconnected from the electric network of the somatic cells which controls the growth and shaping into functional tissues and organs. When the programming of the fused cell combines in a way that it wants to grow and divide while disconnected from the body control network, you get a cancer.

[VIDEO]

Pretty much anything can cause cellular stress, including the normal operation of worn cells in an old body. Cataloguing the strength of the stressors is still useful.

author: infamia
story_title: Don't be fooled–LLMs don't reason
why: Richard Sutton explains why LLMs differ from real reasoning
quote: helped bring order and firm up some of my thoughts and theories.
text:
> This is the problem I have. People are built to be fooled by this stuff - to see something that's not there. Pareidolia but with language.

I really like this metaphor, it hits home that just because you sense something is human-like doesn't make it so. We're wired to respond to those sorts of things.

> When I stumble around trying to explain my thinking

I had similar difficulties expressing my thoughts in an organized way. The video below from Richard Sutton (the father of Reinforcement Learning [which LLMs use extensively in training]), helped bring order and firm up some of my thoughts and theories.

[VIDEO]

>I invariably get hit with the response, Sure, but if it's functionally identical to a coin being magically pulled out your ear, what's the difference if it is or if it isn't?

Not to spoil the video, but it isn't at all functionally equivalent. LLMs are an imperfect and somewhat randomized simulation of what the LLM thinks an average person might say in response to a question. Which is another way of saying, most people will on average get worse answers than if they worked on a problem themselves (but they will get that worse answer from the LLM comparatively quickly). Practical people respond to this positioning fairly well, and for others it still lands a bit since no one wants to think they're below average. That said, I'm still working on my positioning a bit as well!

author: EvanAnderson
story_title: STS-51-F Abort-to-Orbit (1985)
why: KSP simulation of a Space Shuttle RTLS abort
quote: Somebody made a fun (if you like this kind of stuff) simulation of an RTLS abort[2] in Kerbal Space Program.
text:
My "favorite" Space Shuttle abort mode is the Return to Launch Site (RTLS) abort[0] because of the complex energy management procedure necessary to pull it off.

As I understand it the energy management of an RTLS is tenuous because, ultimately, the orbiter is an unpowered glider (with a glide ratio similar to a brick). The limits of stress on the orbiter's airframe are a factor, too.

The orbiter's mass, energy (altitude), and downrange position all have to be in a reasonably tight envelope to make the landing without coming up short or overshooting (there's only so much energy you can bleed off doing S turns).

John Young[1] described an RTLS abort working thru "continuous miracles, interspersed with acts of God".

Somebody made a fun (if you like this kind of stuff) simulation of an RTLS abort[2] in Kerbal Space Program.

I'm very strongly in camp 1. My reaction to this whole bru-ha-ha has been to start trying to build an open source data diode with entry/exit proxies that nets out to less than $100 retail. So far I've determined that while a WaveShare RP2350-ETH seemed like it might be perfect for it, the onboard CH2910 chip just isn't up to the requirements for the various proxies that have to be handled. I'm now moving on to the Raspberry Pi B+, yes, the old one, with no wireless at all, Adafruit still had some in stock. Once I get this working, I'll likely use something like a 6N137 optocoupler for the actual data-diode between two serial ports, with a data fountain handling the egress of data in a hard unidirectional manner.

Given the enormous burn rates that these LLM companies have, surely they could have put everything in an air-gapped network, with some data-diodes proxying out the logging information. It's not rocket surgery. [1,2,3]

> You'd expect diffusion to dilute the pools and yet they seem to last a very long time somewhere on the order of thousands of years.

What I've learned from things like this is that my intuition for when diffusion should work, and how fast, is just busted.

The biggest example in my mind is pyroclastic flows from a volcano. For years (mostly as a kid), I didn't understand what they were because I kept thinking roughly "if it was just gas it couldn't hold together into a coherent flow, right?" Well, as far as I can tell, yeah, they're basically just gas, but really hot and full of rocks. I still don't really get why they hold together instead of poofing out into clouds, except that it has something to do with how they're denser than the surrounding atmosphere. They're sometimes also referred to as "pyroclastic density currents", go figure. [LINK]

Another big one that threw me for a loop as a kid was "warm/cold air masses" interacting in a way that kept their identity. "why does the warm air mass ride up on top of the cool air instead of just mixing?" I guess the answer here is that they're just too big for the mixing to happen faster than the bulk motion.

Anyway, it seems like fluids, especially fluids of very different properties, especially different density, take their time mixing, sometimes long enough to let them act like separate objects in contact for much longer than I, for one, would think. You also don't have the right to have a lawyer be in a room with you and you are compelled to answer all their questions and finally they do not need to tell you why they stopped you.

story_title: Coltrane's Tone Circle
why: Example of Coltrane-like major-third modulation in a standard's bridge
quote: used at moderate tempo in the bridge of the Rogers/Hart tune Have You Met Miss Jones? [1]
text:
The Coltrane Changes pattern of descending through major keys via major thirds is actually used at moderate tempo in the bridge of the Rogers/Hart tune Have You Met Miss Jones? [1] ... which is a standard from a musical haha.

But I acknowledge that in that context, it's an "out there" harmonic adventure which builds tension, to be released when the final section harps on the tonic.

I still think that it's mostly the tempo that makes Giant Steps feel alien. Modulating through major keys by major thirds isn't that exotic, but doing it so quickly that ear just doesn't get a chance to orient itself is.

author: rectang
story_title: Coltrane's Tone Circle
why: Pre-Giant Steps tune modulating through many key centers
quote: like Con Alma [1] by Dizzy Gillespie from 1954
text:
Sure. It's also true that if you speed anything up enough it becomes impossible for anybody to play. But neither of those reductio ad absurdum observations tells us much.

The point is that this Vox presentation and many other articles on the Coltrane changes present them as so revolutionary that improvisers struggle, but on its own that's not true.

There are records which predate Giant Steps which are equally harmonically interesting and challenging and which similarly modulate through many key centers, like Con Alma [1] by Dizzy Gillespie from 1954 or Lush Life [2] by Billy Strayhorn from 1948.

What Coltrane did with Giant Steps was akin to calling for Lush Life at 300 beats per minute.

author: exDM69
story_title: SDF vs. MSDF vs. Slug: GPU Text Rendering
why: Entertaining exploration of font rasterization techniques
quote: This was inspired by this entertaining but not very serious video about font rasterization [0].
text:
As hobby project, I wrote a font rasterizer algorithm (two algorithms actually) that produces pixel perfect anti-aliased images (like Slug) using a similar but different algorithm. Rather than using Slug's clever root classifier for Bezier curves, I subdivide Bezier curves into monotonic sections where evaluating the winding number is much simpler and can be done in parallel for a group of pixels. It works nicely on GPU with warp/wave/subgroup operations and CPU using SIMD.

At first glance, subdividing the Bezier curves sounds like a bad idea (more Beziers to rasterize) but it opens doors for some parallelism, and most Bezier curves that appear in fonts are monotonic in the first place (so the increase is very modest). This was inspired by this entertaining but not very serious video about font rasterization [0].

The first parallelism optimization is checking against the curve bounding box vs. a rectangular (in uv-space) region of pixels, and this can quickly determine if the Bezier needs to be evaluated in the first place. This can be done per GPU warp.

The second optimization works only for rectilinear transformation (no rotation, skew or perspective). Solving the quadratic equation involves a square root and a division (which alone are >30% of the computation), which can be computed for each row and column of pixels instead of for each pixel (2n instead of n^2).

Both optimizations rely on mathematical invariants of monotonicity, ie. the derivative of the Bezier curve m

You can at least say that there hasn't been one software crisis since the 60s. From my understanding the crisis referred to by Dijsktra was in regards to programs being so difficult write in those times that software development couldn't move forward as a field.

This was prior to "Structured programming" catching on which contains the usual constructs of today (for-loops, if statements, etc.). Structured programming somewhat ended that first crisis, once again allowing software to grow in complexity and scope.

We've had other crisis since then and do right now. But they are not the same as that specific crisis. Our programming capacities did increase with the adoption of structured programming.

author: jodrellblank
story_title: Nissan's third generation e-POWER powertrain
why: Explains how Toyota hybrid drivetrains actually work and why they're good.
quote: claims that people misunderstand the purpose, and I had.
text:
> "Just get the EV and skip the awkward half-way step that inherits the most expensive and complicated parts from both designs."

The recent Technology Connections video[1] on Toyota's hybrid drivetrain claims that people misunderstand the purpose, and I had. I assumed battery for stop-start city driving and engine for everything else, but no. Only the motors can move the car which means no gearbox or transmission, which is simpler and cheaper than I had imagined two drivetrains would be. It has a small engine because the battery assists when power demand is high (acceleration) which is cheaper than a pure ICE car and the battery is smaller and cheaper than a pure EV. It (sometimes) starts the engine after pulling away because it needs enough charge to keep power available.

Two extra benefits: regenerative braking reclaims some energy, and the engine can run on the Atkinson-cycle which is too gutless for an ICE car. Both contributing to much better fuel efficiency than an ICE car, while keeping the convenience of easy refuelling instead of recharging.

I feel like you could take all the handwavy comment that are made today to dismiss this caution, and find equal dismissal back then when companies were actively outsourcing the manufacturing.

"I'm coding 10x faster" 
"look at the output velocity per employee"

"we are producing much more (in China)" 
"look at profit / number of (manufacturing) employers"

Seems ok if you're American / Chinese but I'm struggling to understand how the rest can be OK with allowing institutional knowledge to deteriorate while having an active dependency to the former two. We already see this with the tech dependency towards USA and manufacturing competition from China.

author: mogrinz
story_title: Reverse-engineering a $35 backup camera display (AMT630A)
why: Test of a homemade full-size Robby the Robot suit
quote: I built a full-size Robby the Robot suit and discovered I couldn't actually see out of it
text:
This started because I built a full-size Robby the Robot suit and discovered I couldn't actually see out of it ([VIDEO])

I bought a $35 backup camera/display to solve that problem, then discovered that the display contained an AMT630A video processor with a surprisingly capable OSD system. That sent me down a rabbit hole of I2C probing, firmware dumping, register tracing, custom graphics, bitmap formats, hidden factory menus, and eventually figuring out how to use an ESP32 to generate a programmable HUD over the live composite video.

I ended up turning what I learned into an Arduino library, which I've released on GitHub. It supports built-in and custom fonts, multiple OSD windows, 16-color bitmaps, palettes, transparency, and animation. It can also be used with composite video sources other than the camera.

The library and code are here: [LINK]
You can also install directly from the Arduino IDE Library Manager (search for AMT630A)
